articles.title_orig: ASU hockey coach is put on leave; hospitalized player is unlikely to recover, family attorney says
articles.title_zh: ASU hockey coach is put on leave; hospitalized player is unlikely to recover, family attorney says
articles.content_orig:
Arizona State University has placed its hockey coach, Greg Powers, on paid administrative leave after a player collapsed during a workout last month and remains hospitalized.
ASU said assistant coach Mike Corbett will take over for now and that an interim coach would be named "soon." The school did not say how long Powers was expected to remain on leave.
Matthew Mayich, a 21-year-old sophomore from Ontario, Canada, collapsed during a workout on Aug. 20. Robert Carey, an attorney for the Mayich family, has said he is "unlikely to recover," according to CBS affiliate KPHO-TV .
According to a report from the school about the incident, Mayich was taking part in a "wind-down" exercise that involved running with a medicine ball at one of the school's outdoor facilities when he collapsed. The high temperature that day was over 100 degrees, according to the National Weather Service, although the school said the workout took place when the temperature ranged from 86 to 89 degrees.
"When running, Matthew appeared to struggle, and then in rapid succession stumbled, dropped the medicine ball, and fell to the ground. He attempted to get up and resume running but fell to his knees," the report said. Mayich was told to stay down by players and coaches and an athletic trainer tried to use iced towels and cold water to cool him down.
The school said Mayich was initially responsive but that his condition deteriorated.
Mayich's parents, John and Christina, had previously called for the coaches who ran the workout to be put on leave. In a statement Wednesday, they said putting only Powers on leave isn't enough.
"Putting Powers on leave while his best friend of the last decade stays in charge of the locker room doesn't solve the problem," they said in a statement. "If ASU won't remove him, even just to err on the side of player safety, then the interim head coach it has promised should have the authority to place on leave anyone who poses a risk of retaliation against these players."
Seven other players have disputed the school's version of events, saying in a letter sent Tuesday to ASU's president that the outside consultant who ran the workout was not approved in accordance with the school's policy, the workout lasted longer than the school said, the players did not receive sufficient water breaks, and the workout "continued after some of us showed signs of distress."
The students, who chose to remain anonymous for fear of retaliation, stated that Mayich in particular was not given any water breaks and had shown signs of distress before the final exercise during which he collapsed. They also said required emergency equipment, like cold-water immersion tubs, wasn't on the field.
The workout, which the students say was run by Tim Ziesel, a man whom the school described as "an individual who had spoken with the ASU Hockey team in the 2025-26 season about topics of leadership and teamwork," was described in the students' letter as "grueling" and "military-style."
Ziesel, in a statement released by his attorney, said, "There is no such thing as a military style workout other than calisthenics done to a cadence."
"The term 'military style workout' is a term that was made up out of thin air," he said. "The actual workout would be considered easy by a high school varsity football or basketball team. I am a Navy Veteran and I was a head varsity coach for 28 years. The emphasis should be on [the] family of Matthew. They are not served by made up terms."
The students alleged Mayich was left in the sun for several minutes after he collapsed, and "the only cooling on hand was one small cooler holding a few Powerade sideline towels ... squirt bottles that put out a stream of water rather than a spray, and later, after he was moved, a garden hose with warm water."
The students in their letter requested that the staff responsible for the workout be placed on leave pending the results of an independent investigation.
Maricopa County Attorney Rachel Mitchell said Tuesday on social media that the ASU Police Department is investigating the incident, and once that probe is finished, her office will "review this matter at the highest level."

articles.title_orig: MI5 warns UK universities over ‘theft of tech secrets by Chinese front company’
articles.title_zh: MI5 warns UK universities over ‘theft of tech secrets by Chinese front company’
articles.content_orig:
Security service says academics should stop working with and taking grants from firm backed by Chinese intelligence
MI5 China alert will send chill through UK’s cash-strapped universities
MI5 has issued a rare public warning to UK universities that China’s intelligence service is using a front company to pay for research by UK academics and steal the secrets of hi-tech projects.
Britain’s domestic security service said researchers and academics should cease work with the China General Technology Research Institute (CGTRI), sometimes also known as the China Academy of General Technology (CAGT).
MI5 believes the body poses a “significant threat” and is now prepared to say publicly that the CGTRI is a front for Chinese intelligence, namely the Chinese ministry of state security (MSS). It said continued collaboration by UK academics could be prosecuted under the National Security Act 2023.
The Chinese organisation has funded 100 or more academics at a string of universities across the UK, in return for access to the research, which it is alleged found its way back to China’s intelligence service.
On Wednesday, the Chinese embassy in London issued a strongly worded rebuttal, describing the accusations as “imaginary and purely fabricated”. A spokesperson said: “We firmly oppose such baseless allegations and have lodged solemn representations with the UK side.
“Exchanges and collaboration between UK universities and China have always been conducted on a voluntary basis and in compliance with laws and regulations. Such exchanges and collaboration are mutually beneficial.”
The MI5 warning sent a shock wave through the UK university sector, with staff reviewing the implications for existing or future partnerships with China, and experts raising concerns about the rigour of the vetting process in sensitive research collaborations.
Areas of research targeted include AI, cybersecurity, covert communications and steganography – the embedding of secret data in seemingly innocuous files. MI5 believes it has clear evidence of sensitive information being passed back to Chinese intelligence, and the Guardian understands that some British-based academics were given honours and awards by the Chinese as well as research money.
Successive British governments have courted Chinese investment and encouraged academic cooperation. Sam Dunning, the director of the UK-China Transparency group, said: “It is reasonably obvious from the internet that CGTRI was focused on areas of high interest to the military and intelligence services.
“Granted, CGTRI used various aliases and have certainly obscured some funding streams, but as for the UK universities or academics who knew they were dealing with CGTRI, open-source research made clear that CGTRI had military or intelligence links.”
Vice-chancellors who spoke to the Guardian said they were not aware of receiving any funding from the Chinese institute, but warned that individual academics working on joint projects with other universities or third parties may not know the original sources of funding.
Prof Peter Mathieson, vice-chancellor of the University of Edinburgh and the lead for international security for Universities UK, which represents 142 institutions across the UK, said MI5’s warning meant that future collaborations with the CGTRI would be illegal.
“They are saying that anyone who has a link to this institute up until now has not committed any kind of offence, because it’s not previously been said this was a high-risk activity.
“Now that they have said it, we have to sit up and take notice. It’s very much a forward-looking directive.
He added: “I can’t speak for MI5, but I think what they are attempting to say is that people may not realise that the institute they are working with is connected to the security services of the Beijing government. And there’s no reason why anyone should have realised that, because it’s a new piece of information that MI5 has discovered.”
In the alert issued on Wednesday, the Security Service said: “MI5 has identified that the primary purpose of CGTRI is to fund academic research that directly improves MSS technical capability for espionage.”
It said that CGTRI had “very strong ties to the … MSS, China’s civilian intelligence and security service”.
The alert continued: “Many academic institutions and individuals will to date have engaged with CGTRI in good faith given CGTRI’s obfuscated links to MSS.
after newsletter promotion
“UK academic institutions are strongly advised to immediately review any ongoing or planned collaboration with CGTRI. This is to ensure MSS derives no further benefit from UK universities or research institutions. Further, academics are advised to establish the ultimate funding source when conducting any research collaboration with Chinese institutions, to ensure CGTRI is not involved.”
That MI5 has decided on a public alert as a deterrence strategy, rather than trying to pursue every single case, demonstrates the scale of Chinese state espionage targeting the UK. It hopes universities will heed the warning and immediately cease their work with CGTRI.
The Guardian understands that cutting-edge British research on scraping social media (gathering large amounts of information from social sites and apps) is among the data to which MI5 believes Chinese intelligence gained access.
The security minister, Dan Jarvis, demanded universities end ties to the CGTRI. He said: “This alert exposes attempts by Chinese intelligence to covertly benefit from the expertise and research of our academics, undermining our national security and that of our allies.
“I have written to all university vice-chancellors to ensure they support their staff to end all arrangements with this company, preventing further benefit to the Chinese intelligence services and ensuring compliance with the National Security Act.”
Responding to the MI5 alert, Vivienne Stern, the chief executive of Universities UK, said universities took their responsibilities around research security and national security extremely seriously.
“The sector has made significant investments in recent years to strengthen due diligence, risk assessment and research security processes, while continuing to support the international collaboration that is essential to world-leading research and innovation,” she said.
Chinese government filings suggest that CAGT is connected to the China General Technology Group, a major state-owned conglomerate administered directly by the government of China that is also known as Genertec .
The Genertec brand has a UK presence, with a company called Genertec (UK) Ltd, appearing to be owned by the Chinese state.
The British company, which has been registered in the UK for a decade and is based in a shared office address on Southwark Bridge Road, had £5.6m in the bank according to accounts to the end of 2024 – cash that seems to have come exclusively from a single property transaction.

Support for white Afrikaners, anti-communism and others reveals how US redefining what qualifies as human rights
With hours left before the funding expires, the Trump administration is pushing to direct more than $175m of the state department’s flagship human rights fund to a slate of awards that includes a huge $40m grant for an anti-communism fund, support for a group advancing white Afrikaner rights in South Africa, a campaign against Brazil’s supreme court and programs that would reward ideological allies in Europe who protect “western civilizational norms”.
On Wednesday, the state department obligated the funds to the grantees hours before the deadline despite congressional concerns and requests not to do so, according to a source familiar with the negotiations. The state department declined to comment on questions from the Guardian specifically on whether it had obligated the funds and had “blown” holds from Congress due to concerns about the money’s use.
Critics have focused on 43 awards of a combined $176.9m that will bolster rightwing and conservative causes around the world while probably angering US allies over interference in internal politics. The Guardian has seen a sample of the controversial grants, which make up most of the $205m in funding that Congress has appropriated for the entire Human Rights and Democracy Fund (HRDF).
Sources with knowledge of the grant process have told the Guardian that the awards were personally lobbied for by members of the Trump administration, and reflect interests that include JD Vance’s warnings of the collapse of traditional western values in Europe and Stephen Miller’s push against immigration and to support white minorities in countries like South Africa .
“The story for me is the high-level – including White House-directed – attention on these programs,” said a person familiar with the discussions over the democracy awards. “These awards have been briefed at the highest levels of the department and have buy-in from the White House.”
The proposed awards represent a significant shift in US support for dissidents, human rights defenders and civil society groups under authoritarian governments. The new slate includes projects in wealthy nations, and those focused on opposition to regulation, Brexit, migration, anti-communism, Christian protection and opposition to “gender ideology”, offering a window into how the Trump administration is redefining what qualifies as human rights and merits tens of millions of dollars in US foreign assistance.
“Congress appropriated money for the democracy fund on a bipartisan basis to support defenders of human rights, to assist victims of human rights violations and to instead promote the growth of democracy abroad,” said Jeanne Shaheen, the top Democrat on the US Senate committee on foreign relations.
“The Trump administration’s proposals would use taxpayer funds to promote far-right organizations and programs in established democracies. This is a waste of resources and undermines United States values and relations with democratic partners, including allies in Europe.”
The largest award, of $40m, was directed to a consortium led by the Victims of Communism Memorial Foundation (VOC), an anti-communist non-profit that has received far smaller grants in the past. A state department vetting document seen by the Guardian records $96,997 in previous contracts in the last five years between the foundation and the department, all in the 2022 fiscal year, and notes that it had been vetted in 2019 in connection with tickets to the foundation’s gala. The vetting document also identifies Andrew Bremberg, a former Trump White House domestic policy adviser and US ambassador to the UN European office, as a “senior leader” of the foundation.
In July, ProPublica reported that Samuel Samson, a 27-year-old deputy assistant secretary overseeing the new grants, was linked to senior members of VOC through his studies at the Christian conservative Hillsdale College graduate program. (A state department official then told the outlet that the relationship had nothing to do with the grant).
Samson has described the US and Europe as partners in a shared civilizational struggle. Samson toured Austria, the Czech Republic, Hungary and Slovakia last December – all countries that were floated to receive a $2m grant to counter migration weaponized by Russia and Belarus – and criticized NGOs that previous administrations had worked with for promoting what he called radical concepts, including gender theory and DEI.
The state department did not comment on individual grants but said the programs were still in “active deliberation”, that awardees would meet guidelines for federal grants, and that all programming would undergo a “standard and rigorous vetting process by grant professionals”.
“Our programming in Europe aims to support our European allies in defending those rights and principles, along with their civilizational self-confidence and sovereignty from those who seek to undermine them,” a state department official said. “The national security strategy highlights our priorities in Europe which includes advancing political liberty, promoting free speech, and collaborating with European partners to jointly support European revitalization and civilizational self-confidence.”
Under the legislation authorizing the fund, the money must be assigned by 30 September, the end of the fiscal year, when unobligated funds typically lapse. Shaheen, the ranking member of the Senate foreign relations committee, has put a partial “hold” on giving the grants to some of the controversial awardees – setting up a showdown with the state department with just hours left for the money to be obligated.
The Guardian first reported that Trump officials had drawn up no-bid grants aimed at rightwing and anti-immigration causes in Europe. ProPublica similarly reported that there were at least a dozen no-bid grants earmarked for rightwing projects.
The document now shows how much of the fund the plan takes up, and which awards have since been dropped.
A $1m award titled “Countering Lawfare and Censorship in Brazil” would fund civil society groups opposing what it calls judicial overreach and censorship by Brazil’s supreme court. The Trump administration sanctioned the Brazilian justice Alexandre de Moraes last year after lobbying by Eduardo Bolsonaro, son of the former president.
A program titled “Promoting Western Civilization Allies” would be limited to implementers who do not subscribe to “ideologically weaponized accounts of human rights, such as gender ideology”, according to the document, and will receive $2m. It names possible recipients in Poland, Slovakia, the Czech Republic, Hungary, and the Balkans with “anti-communist” and “natural rights” approaches.
One award was allocated to document “democratic backsliding” in Europe tied to “mass and illegal migration” and legislation by “supra-national entities”, while a $1m journalism consortium would push back against designations of “trusted” media outlets. The list also includes $2m for early-warning networks protecting Christians in Nigeria.
And a $3m no-bid award would go to the Jobs Foundation, a UK group run by Matthew Elliott, who led the Vote Leave campaign. The grant, titled “Countering Overregulation to Advance American Investment”, would promote a “common good capitalism index” and pro-business policy, including how the foundation promoted Brexit as a chance to cut the UK’s climate regulations.
The document also shows that a proposed $5m no-bid grant to the Free Speech Union, the British group founded by Toby Young, has been marked “withdrawn”. When the award was first reported in July, Young said the group had never applied for or received US government money (though Trump officials had reportedly met with the group during a European tour late last year).

articles.title_orig: Fed’s Watchdog Finds No Misconduct or Illegal Activity in Costly Renovations
articles.title_zh: Fed’s Watchdog Finds No Misconduct or Illegal Activity in Costly Renovations
articles.content_orig:
WASHINGTON — The Federal Reserve’s independent watchdog said Wednesday it found no reasonable grounds to believe there was a violation of federal law in a multibillion-dollar renovation project that drew criticism from President Donald Trump and short-lived scrutiny from federal prosecutors.
But the central bank’s board “had not effectively executed” a contract and its cost-management provisions, according to a 120-page report from the Office of the Inspector General for the Board of Governors of the Federal Reserve System. Still, the report “did not identify administrative misconduct” nor any “reasonable grounds to believe that a violation of federal criminal law had occurred.”
Later Wednesday, Trump blamed the cost overruns on former Fed chair Jerome Powell, long a target of the president’s ire.
“This is Jerome Powell’s fault, and he should be forced to resign, IMMEDIATELY! If he doesn’t resign, he should be sued, at the highest level, by the United States Government, for either corruption or incompetence, both of which are completely unacceptable,” the president wrote in a post on Truth Social .
An attorney for Powell didn’t immediately respond to a request for comment.
The inspector general’s report follows a more than yearlong review into the construction site on the central bank’s Washington, D.C., campus, which became a fixation of the Trump administration as the president also pressured Powell to cut interest rates. Powell, whom Trump nominated for the top Fed job during his first term, remained on the Fed’s board after Kevin Warsh took over as chair in May.
Even after four years of construction and over $2 billion in awarded construction costs, the Fed board had “not established a guaranteed maximum price” for the project, and had set up “insufficient” internal project governance to manage a project of such “magnitude and complexity,” the watchdog said.
Several components of the renovation’s design that drew scrutiny — the building’s marble, water features and a garden terrace — “did not materially contribute to subsequent cost increases,” the watchdog found. The removal of four water features from the renovation plans would not result in significant cost savings, one official told the watchdog, because landscaping and other costs would be needed to replace the fountains.
The watchdog said cost overruns resulted from “inflation, limited subcontractor bidding, substantial Board interior fit-out design changes, and challenging site conditions.”
Moving from a design that focused on closed offices over open workspaces after construction began, the watchdog found, was a “clear example of the consequences of ineffective project management” and “extended the project’s duration and its exposure to inflationary pressures.”
In a letter to Inspector General Michael Horowitz, Warsh wrote that as chairman of the board he agreed about the need to complete the work “in the most efficient and transparent way possible” and said the General Services Administration would be the project executive, effective immediately.
Warsh, who had also been a critic of the renovation, said the American people were owed “a prudent and conscientious use of public funds.”
The GSA is the federal agency tasked with overseeing the federal government’s office buildings, technology services and real estate.
The renovation became a point of contention during a June 25, 2025, Senate hearing. Sen. Tim Scott, R-S.C., asked Powell about the Fed’s renovation project, which caught the White House’s attention.
Scott accused Powell of having “spent billions on lavish renovations” that included “rooftop terraces, custom elevators that open into VIP dining rooms, white marble finishes and even a private art collection.”
Powell denied Scott’s accusations.
“There’s no [VIP] dining room. There’s no new marble. We took down the old marble, we’re putting it back up. We’ll have to use new marble where some of the old marble broke. But there’s no special elevators. There’s just old elevators that have been there. There are no new water features. There’s no beehives, and there’s no roof terrace gardens,” the then-Fed chair said.
On Wednesday, Scott he welcomes the inspector general’s findings. “Inflation does not change the Fed’s responsibility to manage its resources prudently and be accountable to Congress,” he wrote in a statement. The Senate Banking Committee, which Scott chairs, “will continue rigorous oversight to ensure the Fed is transparent and stays focused on its mission,” he added.
Shortly after the June hearing, Trump’s Office of Management and Budget director, Russell Vought, wrote Powell a letter saying that the president was “extremely troubled by your management of the Federal Reserve System,” citing the renovation.
“Comparable federal building renovations cost many orders of magnitude less than the office you are building for yourself on the taxpayer’s dime,” Vought added. He later likened the office building renovation to “a palace.”
The Federal Reserve System is not funded by taxpayer money. It is self-funded by the fees it charges on services such as processing checks. It is also funded by the interest it earns on its vast bond portfolio.
Powell denied Vought’s allegations, saying that the central bank had “taken great care to ensure the project is carefully overseen since it was first approved by the Board in 2017.”
As noted by Powell, the project was first approved by the Fed’s entire seven-member Board of Governors. Powell became Fed chair in 2018 after Trump nominated him in late 2017.
The Trump administration did not let up on its campaign against Powell. On July 24, Trump himself made an unprecedented and surprise visit to the Fed’s construction site .
Touring the project alongside Powell and Scott, the president began suggesting that the price tag had ballooned even further. Powell sharply responded, “I haven’t heard that.” Handed a piece of paper by Trump, Powell said that Trump was including a previously completed building project in his new, higher cost estimate.
The Fed also launched a website, which noted that the price tag of the project had risen beyond its first estimate due to changes to the design after voluntarily consulting review boards, and the rising cost of materials, equipment and labor. It also said unforeseen circumstances, such as “more asbestos than anticipated,” contributed.
Still, throughout the year, Trump openly mused about firing Powell, which sometimes rattled markets. A Federal Reserve chair has never been fired before.
After months of more muted complaints about the project, in January a new revelation about it rocked Washington.
In an extraordinary video statement posted to the Fed’s social media pages on a Sunday night in January, Powell announced that “the Department of Justice served the Federal Reserve with grand jury subpoenas.”
He said a criminal probe had been launched against him and the central bank over his earlier Senate testimony.
“No one — certainly not the chair of the Federal Reserve — is above the law,” Powell said. “But this unprecedented action should be seen in the broader context of the administration’s threats and ongoing pressure.” He added: “This is about whether the Fed will be able to continue to set interest rates based on evidence and economic conditions — or whether instead monetary policy will be directed by political pressure or intimidation.”
Those subpoenas were later blocked by a judge , who said that Trump’s handpicked U.S. attorney in D.C. had “produced essentially zero evidence to suspect Chair Powell of a crime.”
But the damage had already been done. Trump’s U.S. attorney for D.C., Jeanine Pirro — whose aides tried to tour the Fed amid the investigation — said her office closed its probe and referred the matter to the inspector general. The watchdog already had an open inquiry at Powell’s request.

articles.title_zh: Arizona State places men’s hockey coach Greg Powers on paid leave - The Athletic
articles.content_orig:
Arizona State men’s hockey coach Greg Powers was placed on paid leave Wednesday after sophomore Matthew Mayich was placed on life support last month following a team workout.
Assistant coach Mike Corbett will temporarily replace Powers, and he will coach the team in their first two games of the season this weekend.
Corbett was present when Mayich collapsed.
The news comes two days after seven players asked university president Michael Crow to remove Powers and his staff as further investigation unfurls on the events leading up to Mayich’s hospitalization.
Mayich suffered “exertional heat stroke that caused a lack of oxygen to the brain” during a workout on August 20, his family attorney Rob Carey told ESPN.
He is not expected to recover .
The workout during which Mayich collapsed was led by an ex-Green Beret, Tim Ziesel.
Per multiple accounts, the workout was military-style and forced those lagging behind to do extra work in extreme heat.
Team personnel asked for permission for Ziesel to speak with the team, but allegedly never submitted his training plan for review with the strength and conditioning coach.
Carey also called for the ASU coaching staff to be placed on leave so the players could be free to speak on what happened without fear of repercussions.
The events surrounding the Aug. 20 workout are still under review by the university and under investigation by the ASU Police Department.
Mayich’s parents, John and Christina, also called for the coaching staff to be removed.
“We’ve heard some things about what our family wants that aren’t right, so we want to be clear,” their statement read. “We want this team to have a great season, and we’ll be cheering for you. But the coaches who ran that workout on August 20 need to be removed while an independent investigation gets to the truth. The players shouldn’t have to worry about retaliation from the people they report to every day.”
Arizona State opens its season at Lindenwood University in Missouri on Friday and Saturday.

For the fiscal first quarter, Micron said it expects revenue of about $61.5 billion and adjusted earnings per share of $38.15. Analysts polled by LSEG had expected $35.40 in adjusted earnings per share on $57 billion in revenue.
Micron's stock has soared more than 500% in the past year, benefiting from a worldwide supply crunch caused by historic levels of demand for memory chips needed for artificial intelligence models and workloads. The shortage has led to a spike in memory costs and resulted in increased prices for  consumer electronics like Apple 's iPads and MacBooks.
Hendi Susanto, portfolio at Gabelli Funds, said in an email after the release that it was "another strong beat and raise for Micron." Susanto wrote.
"At this point, I have not heard any negative data points pointing to the memory cycle reversing toward a decline anytime soon for the foreseeable future,"
Micron is the only U.S.-based maker of high-bandwidth memory, HBM, made up of stacks of general-purpose dynamic random-access memory, or DRAM. Fourth-quarter DRAM revenue increased 343% from a year ago to $39.8 billion, representing 73% of total sales.
CEO Sanjay Mehrotra said on the earnings call that the company has a "strong roadmap for future HBM products" and is working with Nvidia on the industry's "first custom HBM implementation."
Net income in the latest quarter climbed to $37.7 billion, or $32.87 per share, from $3.2 billion, or $2.83 per share a year ago.
Advanced graphics and central processors from chip giants like Nvidia and AMD need increasing amounts of HBM to handle AI workloads, and the world's leading providers can't make enough.
That's why Micron is investing $250 billion to build two new campuses for making HBM. The largest broke ground in Clay, New York, in January, while its first new fab in Boise, Idaho, is scheduled to come online next year.
HBM leaders SK Hynix and Samsung are also in the midst of massive new HBM factory buildouts in their home country of South Korea. Micron holds the smallest HBM market share of the three, but its market cap has still topped $1.2 trillion.
Mehrotra participated in a summit on AI regulation hosted by President Donald Trump on Tuesday, days after attending a White House dinner with Chinese President Xi Jinping on his first visit to the U.S. in more than a decade.

articles.title_orig: Elon Musk, Palmer Luckey and Newt Gingrich to help Pentagon with warfare initiative, Hegseth says
articles.title_zh: Elon Musk, Palmer Luckey and Newt Gingrich to help Pentagon with warfare initiative, Hegseth says
articles.content_orig:
The Pentagon is tapping Tesla and SpaceX CEO Elon Musk , defense technology entrepreneur and Anduril co-founder Palmer Luckey and former House Speaker Newt Gingrich to identify the military capabilities, technologies and weapons the U.S. may need in future wars, Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth said Wednesday.
The initiative, dubbed Project Meridian, will spend 120 days looking years and decades ahead at how warfare could change and what capabilities the U.S. military will need to maintain a technological edge.
"Project Meridian, the future of warfare, is not about developing new strategies or new policies," Hegseth said. Instead, he said, its purpose is to "identify the domains that we must conquer, and capabilities we must master."
Hegseth said the effort will focus on “discovering, developing, and fielding” weapons and systems that future U.S. troops may need on battlefields ranging “from under the Earth to beyond the moon.” He announced the initiative during a "State of the Force" address to junior officers and enlisted leaders at Marine Corps Base Quantico in Virginia.
Pentagon technology chief Emil Michael will oversee the project, with Musk, Luckey and Gingrich as co-leads and a broader team drawn from government, industry, academia and the policy world, Hegseth said.
None of the three co-leads has served in the U.S. military. Musk moved to Canada as a teenager in part, he has said , to avoid compulsory military service in South Africa.
The role puts Musk and Luckey in prime position to help identify the military’s future technology needs while their companies compete for billions in DOD business.
Musk's SpaceX holds a plethora of Pentagon contracts. In May, the Space Force awarded the company a $4.16 billion contract to build satellites designed to track and target airborne threats, just days after awarding SpaceX another $2.29 billion contract for a military satellite communications network.
Luckey's Anduril develops autonomous weapons and other military technology. The Marine Corps awarded the company a contract worth up to $642 million in 2025 for counter-drone systems.
The announcement was part of a broader Pentagon push into autonomous warfare including plans announced Wednesday for a new four-star Autonomous Warfare Command aimed at scaling autonomous and robotic systems across the military.
Anduril, SpaceX, Tesla and Gingrich did not immediately respond to requests for comment.

articles.title_orig: Passengers foil bid to crash Dubai-Tel Aviv flight, Israel says, after co-pilot-on-pilot stabbing
articles.title_zh: Passengers foil bid to crash Dubai-Tel Aviv flight, Israel says, after co-pilot-on-pilot stabbing
articles.content_orig:
A plane carrying passengers from an earlier flydubai flight that was diverted to Saudi Arabia arrives at Ben Gurion Airport on Wednesday in Tzafria, Israel. Earlier, their flight from the United Arab Emirates was diverted to Saudi Arabia after a violent altercation in the cockpit. A second plane was sent to Saudi Arabia to retrieve the stranded passengers and return them to Israel. Erik Marmor/Getty Images hide caption
TEL AVIV, Israel, and RIYADH, Saudi Arabia — One pilot stabbed another pilot on a flydubai flight headed to Tel Aviv on Wednesday, and may have tried to crash the plane of mostly Israeli passengers, Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu said.
Netanyahu said a passenger recounted that as the plane "went into a spin and began to plunge," passengers and crew members got into the cockpit and subdued the attacker as he was "sabotaging the aircraft's systems."
Flydubai said in a statement that an "altercation occurred in the flight deck" of flight FZ 1073, traveling from Dubai, United Arab Emirates, to Tel Aviv. It said the flight crew secured the aircraft and diverted the plane to make an emergency landing at an airport in Tabuk, Saudi Arabia. There were no reports of injuries to passengers.
Passengers later recounted frantic moments aboard the plane. The aviation tracking site Flightradar24 said data shows the plane descended more than 14,000 feet in under 30 seconds — way faster than normal.
Passengers who experienced an emergency landing in Saudi Arabia during a flight on flydubai, arrive at Ben Gurion International Airport, near Tel Aviv, Israel, Wednesday. Ariel Schalit/AP hide caption
Netanyahu said the Saudi authorities arrested the suspected attacker and are questioning him. Saudi Arabia did not immediately confirm the arrest, but the Saudi transportation safety authority said officials are investigating the incident.
A statement from Cluster2 , the Saudi company that manages the country's airports, said the flight's captain and first officer, the co-pilot, were being treated for injuries in a hospital.
Flydubai airline said the motives behind the incident were unknown and remain subject to a formal investigation. The United Arab Emirates' civil aviation authority also said, through the state-run Emirates News Agency , that it is investigating the "causes and circumstances of the incident."
Israeli Defense Minister Israel Katz initially called it "an attempted jihadist terrorist attack," without providing details. Netanyahu described it as "a serious security incident."
There was no official identification of the suspected attacker.
The Israeli and Indian governments identified the pilot who was attacked as Indian national Smit Machchhar, and praised his bravery.
"Despite being stabbed and seriously injured, he fought back, resisted, opened the cockpit door, and enabled passengers and crew to overpower the attacker — preventing a catastrophic mid-air disaster," Netanyahu said . "He is a true hero."
This man is a hero. Captain Smit Machchhar, the Indian captain of flydubai Flight 1073, fought back after being stabbed in the cockpit. Despite being severely injured, he managed to unlock the cockpit door - allowing Israeli passengers and the Emirati crew to intervene and save… pic.twitter.com/x4W3mtQkag
The passengers have since been flown from Saudi Arabia to Israel, on a different plane from their earlier flight that had made the emergency landing.
Passengers who experienced an emergency landing in Saudi Arabia during a flydubai flight arrive at Ben Gurion International Airport, near Tel Aviv, Israel, Wednesday. Ariel Schalit/AP hide caption
Israel's Ben Gurion International Airport outside Tel Aviv was full of journalists awaiting the arrival of the passengers. There were also many families, some with balloons and flowers to welcome their loved ones after a scary experience.
The passengers slowly emerged through the arrivals door dragging suitcases behind them, some crying, some smiling, looking relieved or exhausted.
Holding balloons people wait for the arrival of passengers at Ben Gurion International Airport, near Tel Aviv, Israel, Wednesday. Ariel Schalit/AP hide caption
Dan Zoler was traveling with his wife and two small children on the flight. He told NPR that after the pilot was stabbed, he saw three passengers throw themselves on the co-pilot who carried out the attack, and capture him. He said another pilot on the plane took the controls and landed the plane in Saudi Arabia.
Throughout the ordeal, Zoler said he was trying to distract his young son, telling him this is not normal.
"I told him that it's something that happened like once in 25 years. That I want him to be calm. And we are happy to come back," he said smiling, patting his son on the head.
Flights between Israel and the United Arab Emirates are a main connection for vacationers and happen several times a day. Flydubai said it was suspending its flights to and from Israel while authorities investigate the incident.
This comes at a sensitive political moment in Israel with national elections less than a month away, a vote that will determine whether Netanyahu remains prime minister. He has been campaigning on the notion that he alone can protect Israelis from security threats.

articles.title_zh: Paramount-WBD Merger Is A Go As Judge Approves Legal Settlement, Last Hurdle To Close
articles.content_orig:
A California judge on Wednesday formally approved Paramount Skydance’s settlement with California and other states, the final hurdle required for it to close its $110 billion takeover of Warner Bros. Discovery.
The seismic merger will bring together the likes of CBS News and CNN, HBO Max and Paramount+ and storied film studios Warner Bros. and Paramount Pictures.
Shortly after the judge’s approval, David Ellison, the CEO and controlling shareholder of Paramount Skydance, announced that Mattel CEO Ynon Kreiz would become co-CEO of the combined media giant.
Kreiz will join the company on Oct. 5, indicating that the deal will likely close on that date or shortly after.
“As Chairman & CEO, Ellison will lead all strategy, creative and technology while Kreiz, as Co-CEO will oversee the Company’s day-to-day operations and integration of the combined businesses,” the statement said.
Several outlets also reported this week that Paramount’s streaming chief Cindy Holland is departing the studio and Casey Bloys, HBO’s chief, will take on a new role running the combined streaming operations.
After the deal was approved by the U.S. Justice Department , the European Commission and dozens of other countries worldwide, it was held back by a lawsuit led by California’s democratic attorney general Rob Bonta.
Bonta and other state attorneys general worried that the deal, if completed, would reduce competition and potential imperil the journalistic independence of CNN.
Paramount Skydance, led by Ellison, reached a deal with the states on Sept. 21, which will require the combined company to release at least 30 films a year and set up an editorial board to oversee both CNN and CBS News.
Larry Ellison, the father of Paramount CEO David Ellison, is a close Trump ally. He is personally backing the deal with tens of billions of dollars of his own fortune.
After acquiring Paramount, David Ellison appointed former New York Times opinion writer Bari Weiss to run CBS News, who has clashed with longtime correspondents and faced accusations of meddling with their editorial independence.
The merged company pledged it will invest more than $1 billion in U.S. film production and worker training.
The companies did not immediately respond to a request for comment.
Judge Araceli Martínez-Olguín’s approval comes just hours before a so-called “ticking fee” kicks in for Paramount Skydance.
In order to build confidence in their merger plan earlier this year, Paramount agreed to pay Warner Bros. Discovery shareholders 25 cents per share each quarter if the transaction did not close by Sept. 30. That penalty would be worth more than $600 million every three months.
“The parties reached their agreement following highly contested, however brief, litigation, and they reached their agreement following what they report to have been several rounds of in-depth negotiations,” Martínez-Olguín wrote in the order.
Some groups that opposed the merger, such as the “Block The Merger” coalition , urged that the deal between the companies and states be rejected.
The group criticized the state attorneys general for what they called an “about-face” after suing to stop the deal. “The brief argues that small business owners and independent contractors will not receive the same handouts that members of major unions will if the consent decree is not upheld.”
“As for the so-called remedies the settlement offers, they do nothing to protect fair competition,” the group added.
Shares of both Paramount Skydance and Warner Bros. Discovery closed near their highest levels of the day following the news. Paramount shares have been beaten down by more than 20% since the start of the year as the merger remained in limbo.
Steve Kopack is a senior reporter at NBC News covering business and the economy.

Carnegie Mellon University just received a historic $3 billion donation from Citadel CEO Ken Griffin.
Carnegie Mellon, which is located in Pittsburgh , announced the gift Wednesday morning. The university says it intends to use $2 billion to open a new campus in Miami , called Carnegie Mellon University Miami.
“We are deeply grateful to Ken Griffin for his extraordinary vision, partnership and belief in what Carnegie Mellon can achieve,” CMU President Farnam Jahanian said in a statement.
Construction is scheduled to begin in 2027 and should be open to new students in 2028, presuming there are no major regulatory hurdles, according to the Pittsburgh Post-Gazette .
Griffin bought the 35 acres in Wynwood, Florida, where the university will be built, for $1.1 billion from real estate developer Moishe Mana.
Mana said that the sale is the largest land assemblage deal in Florida history.
The campus is expected to support more than 3,500 undergraduate, master's and PhD students, plus approximately 300 faculty members and more than 600 staff.
The university said in a statement that the new school will focus its education on confronting “societal challenges” rather than on traditional academic majors.
The statement said it will focus on “challenge areas spanning human health and biological discovery; national security and strategic capabilities; energy and climate resilience; and advanced manufacturing and industrial transformation.”
The university reportedly had to “rethink” how it operates to respond to the rise of AI.
“Artificial intelligence represents one of the defining intellectual developments of our time, and it demands that we rethink how we educate students, conduct research and partner with others,” Jahanian said.
The final $1 billion of the donation will go to support Carnegie Mellon's Pittsburgh campus. Approximately half will be used to boost the university's highest priority needs, and another half will be invested in its School of Computer Science, which will be renamed the Kenneth C. Griffin School of Computer Science in his honor.
CMU said that the donation is the largest individual donor gift ever given to a university. Before Griffin’s gift, the largest individual donation to a university was Michael Bloomberg’s $1.8 billion donation to Johns Hopkins University in 2018.
This isn’t Griffin’s first investment in South Florida. He attended high school in the region, and moved Citadel’s headquarters from Chicago to Miami in 2022. He explained the move at the time by insisting that Florida had a better corporate environment than Illinois.
He said earlier this year he planned to give fewer resources to Citadel’s presence in New York and more to its efforts in South Florida. He made that decision following a public spat with New York Mayor Zohran Mamdani over a wealth tax in April.
While discussing his proposed tax in April, Mamdani called out Griffin directly, noting that he maintained a $238 million penthouse in the city while others were struggling to find homes due to a lack of affordable housing.
“We went to Miami and revised our building plan to make it a bigger office building,” Griffin said in May. “What the mayor of New York has made clear to my partners, and principally my New York partners, is that we need to double down on our bet in Miami.”

The Federal Trade Commission has opened an investigation into OpenAI, Anthropic and other artificial intelligence companies over the potential dangers posed by their products, an agency spokesperson confirmed to CNBC.
The probe adds to the mounting scrutiny that OpenAI and Anthropic have been facing over their safety practices, especially after industry researchers warned about how the companies' AI models could cause catastrophic harm . OpenAI stunned the industry in July when it disclosed that its agents broke out of a testing environment and hacked into open-source platform Hugging Face .
The FTC spokesperson declined to name any other companies that are being investigated. The New York Post was first to report the probe.
Representatives for OpenAI and Anthropic did not immediately respond to CNBC's request for comment.
Earlier this month, Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei rocked the tech sector by urging AI companies to slow how quickly they improve their most advanced models and calling for stronger government oversight. He published a three-step proposal aimed at tempering the pace of development without "sacrificing commercial advantage or the United States' lead in AI."
Several of Amodei's competitors, including OpenAI CEO Sam Altman and SpaceX CEO Elon Musk , expressed support for his proposal, while others, including Meta CEO Mark Zuckerberg and Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang, argued that individual companies should be responsible for ensuring the safety of their products.
President Donald Trump convened top executives from Alphabet , Meta , SpaceX , Nvidia, Palantir , Anthropic, OpenAI and other companies on Tuesday to discuss the issue. The group signed a short voluntary, nonbinding accord, which says that "every company is responsible for developing its own technology safely and in a way that builds trust with customers and the public."
"We all need to work together to make sure that we can win, and we can win safely," Amodei said outside the White House on Tuesday. "If we do this right, if we work with the president and everyone here, we can win safely."

Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu has thanked an Indian pilot, who was stabbed by a co-pilot, for saving 174 people on board the Flydubai Dubai-Tel Aviv flight that made an emergency landing in Saudi Arabia.
“My salute to the Indian pilot Captain Smit Machchhar for his extraordinary bravery,” Netanyahu wrote on his official X account on Wednesday evening.
He said that despite being stabbed and seriously injured, Machchhar “fought back, resisted, opened the cockpit door, and enabled passengers and crew to overpower the attacker – preventing a catastrophic mid-air disaster”.
“He saved the lives of 174 people, including Israeli citizens and other nationals,” Netanyahu said, adding that he wished the pilot “a speedy and full recovery”.
“He is a true hero,” Netanyahu said.
The co-pilot of the flight, who is accused of stabbing Machchhar in an alleged attempt to take control of the aircraft, remains unidentified, but Netanyahu said he was arrested after the plane landed in Saudi Arabia.
India’s embassy in Riyadh said “the brave Indian pilot of Flydubai” Smit Machchhar was, “admitted in a hospital in Tabuk city in northwest Saudi Arabia and receiving necessary medical attention”, in a post on X.
The embassy said it was awaiting a full update on the pilot’s health but that “he is reported to be in stable condition”.
Flydubai flight FZ1073 transmitted an emergency alert shortly after takeoff from Dubai on Wednesday morning, making an emergency landing in Saudi Arabia’s Tabuk airport with all passengers safe and accounted for, according to the airline.
Flight-tracking data from the Flightradar24 website indicated the flight was a Boeing 737 Max 8 aircraft.
A rescue flight – operated by Flydubai – flew all passengers from Tabuk to their final destination, Tel Aviv’s Ben Gurion airport at 15:34 GMT.
They were received at the airport by Netanyahu, in a display the Israeli opposition leader Yair Lapid called “cheap politics”,  in the run-up to this month’s elections.

I wanted to understand what it takes to do that work well, so I spent a few days with the community response program in Durham, N.C.
From the back of their minivan, I watched responders handle 911 calls about things like trespassing and panhandling. They doled out bottled water, snacks and fresh socks, and defused some tough situations: An agitated man refusing to leave a parking lot, a paranoid man asking to go to the hospital, a woman needing a safer place to live.
But they often had few long-term solutions to offer.
Researchers told me this tension is common. The goal after 2020 was to avoid more police killings, not solve problems like homelessness. Now, Durham and dozens of other cities are wrestling with this bigger question: Is success resolving the crisis? Or is it to offer a path to stability, so that eventually fewer 911 calls are made in the first place?

articles.title_orig: Federal court halts execution of Christa Pike in 11th hour
articles.title_zh: Federal court halts execution of Christa Pike in 11th hour
articles.content_orig:
A federal appeals court has temporarily stopped Tennessee from executing death row inmate Christa Pike , intervening less than two hours before she was due to receive a lethal injection.
The 6th US Circuit Court of Appeals granted what it called a “short stay of execution” on Wednesday while judges consider Pike’s argument that evidence of sexual abuse she experienced as a child was not properly weighed when she was sentenced.
Tennessee officials quickly turned to the US Supreme Court, asking the justices to lift the stay and allow the execution to proceed.
Pike, 50, had been scheduled to die at Riverbend Maximum Security Institution in Nashville. Had the execution gone ahead, she would have been the first woman executed by Tennessee in more than two centuries.
She was sentenced to death for the 1995 killing of Colleen Slemmer, a 19-year-old classmate at a Knoxville vocational centre.
Pike was 18 when she, her 17-year-old boyfriend Tadaryl Shipp, and another teenager tortured and killed Slemmer. Pike and Shipp were later convicted of first-degree murder. Shipp received a life sentence with the possibility of parole.
Pike’s lawyers have argued that her childhood was marked by violence, neglect and sexual abuse, including rapes when she was 11 and 17 years old. They also cited her later diagnoses of bipolar disorder and post-traumatic stress disorder in seeking to have her sentence reduced to life without parole.
Tennessee Governor Bill Lee rejected that clemency request. Slemmer’s mother, May Martinez, has publicly supported the execution.
The case has also attracted international scrutiny, with a group of United Nations human rights experts calling for Pike’s death sentence to be commuted.
Women have accounted for just 18 of the 1,683 executions carried out in the US since capital punishment resumed in 1976. Pike’s case is more unusual still: If the execution ultimately proceeds, she would be the only person in Tennessee’s modern death penalty era put to death for a crime committed as a teenager.

articles.title_orig: Democrats Block Stock-Trading Bill, Denying the G.O.P. a Pre-Midterm Win
articles.title_zh: Democrats Block Stock-Trading Bill, Denying the G.O.P. a Pre-Midterm Win
articles.content_orig:
Washington — A Republican-led effort to approve a House-passed stock trading bill fell short in the Senate on Wednesday, with Democrats arguing the restrictions don't go far enough while pushing back against a voter ID provision that they argue would gut mail voting.
In a 53 to 47 vote that fell along party lines, the measure failed to reach a 60-vote threshold needed to advance.
The bill, known as the Stop Insider Trading Act, passed the House in July with the support of all Republicans and 13 Democrats. It would prohibit lawmakers, their spouses and dependent children, from purchasing publicly traded stocks, while requiring that they publicly disclose each intended sale at least a week in advance to limit their ability to profit off insider information.
But Democrats argued that the bill doesn't go far enough, urging that an outright ban is needed for members of Congress — along with the president and members of his administration.
"The Republican toothless stock-trading bill is as ineffective as a screen door on a submarine," Senate Minority Leader Chuck Schumer said on the Senate floor ahead of the vote. "And let's be clear: they don't even want it to pass. They designed the bill to fail."
The New York Democrat railed against the legislation earlier this week, while noting it wouldn't apply to the executive branch. He claimed that Republicans "carved the White House out of their supposed crack down on corruption."
Democrats also saw the bill's provision requiring voters to show photo identification when voting in federal elections as a poison pill designed to prompt them to vote against the more popular stock-trading restrictions. The unrelated provision was included in the bill as President Trump has put pressure on Congress to approve elections-related legislation ahead of the midterms.
GOP leaders moved ahead with the vote on Wednesday as senators prepare to leave town to hit the campaign trail, bringing up the vote alongside another bill aimed at shielding Americans from energy costs attributed to data centers later in the day. The votes, which were expected to fall short, aimed to put Democrats on the record on the issues at a time when Senate Republicans face several races that have grown more competitive, putting control of the upper chamber next year into question.
Senate Majority Leader John Thune, a South Dakota Republican, called the bill a "common-sense piece of legislation," pointing to its limits on stock trading and the voter ID requirement.
"It's a pretty simple measure," Thune said. "But an important way to ensure that members of Congress are held to the standards that America should be able to expect of their representatives."
Lawmakers have pursued a number of efforts to ban congressional stock trading in recent years. But Schumer argued that the latest bill "isn't a stock-trading ban, it's Republicans' last-ditch effort to save face." If Republicans want to ban stock trading, the New York Democrat said his caucus is "ready to go."

articles.title_zh: S&P 500 rises after data shows inflation slowed last month: Live updates
articles.content_orig:
Treasury yields wavered as traders weighed lighter-than-expected U.S. inflation data for August as they awaited the September jobs report due later in the week.
The 2-year Treasury note yield was last little changed at 4.895%, while the 10-year Treasury yield was more than 4 basis points higher at 5.298%, recovering after a brief pullback earlier in the session. The benchmark yield traded near 2007 highs. The 30-year Treasury bond was up nearly 4 basis points at 5.632%, or around its highest level since 2002.
One basis point equals 0.01%, and yields and prices move in opposite directions.
Consumer prices were reported Wednesday to have posted a smaller-than-expected increase in August compared to the same period a year ago, according to the Federal Reserve's primary measure of inflation.
The personal consumption expenditures price index increased a seasonally adjusted 0.3% last month, putting the 12-month gain at 3.4%, the Commerce Department reported Wednesday. Economists surveyed by Dow Jones had been looking for increases of 0.3% and 3.7% respectively.
"Net, net, the inflation fire is not burning as hot as markets expected in August, and bond yields are adjusting their sails as investors rethink exactly how many Fed rate hikes might be needed to keep inflation moving back down to target," Christopher Rupkey, chief economist at FWDBONDS, wrote in response to the latest release.
Excluding food and energy, PCE posted a 0.2% increase in August that put the annual core level at 3%. The respective forecasts were for 0.3% and 3.3%.
Though the Fed officially follows the headline PCE number, officials generally consider the core reading a better gauge of longer-term inflation trends.
The good news on inflation Wednesday came after recent commentary from Federal Reserve officials led to a repricing of monetary policy expectations. At one point this month, traders priced in a more than 80% chance of a quarter-point rate hike in October. Those odds sat around 37% after Wednesday's release, with traders pushing the next expected increase to December, according to the CME Group's FedWatch tool.
Yields initially moved lower on the data, though they turned back higher as traders began looking ahead to the September U.S. jobs report, due Friday at 8:30 a.m. ET. Economists expect the economy added 84,000 jobs this month.
If Friday's numbers come in hotter than expected — as did Wednesday's ADP private payrolls report — it could send yields higher.

articles.title_orig: Senate Democrats block House-passed data center bill aimed at addressing energy costs
articles.title_zh: Senate Democrats block House-passed data center bill aimed at addressing energy costs
articles.content_orig:
Washington — Senate Democrats on Wednesday blocked a GOP-led effort to advance a bill aimed at shielding Americans from energy costs attributed to data centers, despite the bill securing widespread bipartisan support in the House earlier this month.
In a 57 to 43 vote, all but four Democrats — Sens. Maggie Hassan of New Hampshire, Amy Klobuchar of Minnesota and Jon Ossoff and Raphael Warnock of Georgia — opposed the measure, arguing that the bill would make the protections for Americans "optional."
"While Americans are demanding real guardrails on AI and data centers, Republicans are offering a toothless messaging bill," Senate Minority Leader Chuck Schumer said. "We need real action on data centers, and what do Republicans decide all of a sudden to push forward? A bill that is totally optional."
The outcome denies Republicans a legislative victory just weeks before the midterm elections. Voters across the U.S. have become increasingly opposed to the construction of data centers, which provide the computing power needed to fuel the AI boom. But Republicans argued that the vote would put Democrats on the record on the issue that has gained traction in recent months.
The bill, titled the Ratepayer Protection Act , seeks to put the costs of new energy infrastructure used for data centers on companies, rather than passing costs on to consumers. But it would only require state utility regulators to consider standards to hold companies responsible for the costs, which Senate Democrats argue doesn't go far enough.
The measure passed the House earlier this month in a 417 to 3 vote.
Asked about House Democrats' support for the measure, and why Senate Democrats aren't on the same page, Schumer said "we don't vote for frauds."
Schumer stressed that the measure sets up a voluntary system, saying, "Not a single company has to comply with it." He argued that if Republicans wanted a real solution, including GOP Sen. Jon Husted, who has led the push in the Senate, they should take up legislation put forward by one of his Democratic colleagues "that is real and has teeth."
"They want it optional, which means zero," Schumer said. "We want it mandatory."
Husted is locked in a competitive Senate race in Ohio against former Sen. Sherrod Brown, and has faced scrutiny for his previous support for data centers. The Senate GOP campaign arm warned in a memo last month that more than anything else, the data center issue is the "anchor hanging around Husted's neck."
Earlier this month, Husted sought to approve the same bill under unanimous consent, which gives any single lawmaker the power to block its passage. But Sen. Martin Heinrich of New Mexico, the top Democrat on the Senate Energy and Natural Resources Committee, proposed that the Senate instead pass his own bill that he said is "what is needed to start to bring down energy prices." Ohio's other senator objected to Heinrich's bill.
Wednesday's vote came as senators are preparing to leave town this week and hit the campaign trail. Senate Republicans teed up the vote alongside an effort to pass legislation to limit congressional stock trading, which Democrats also blocked.
Speaking on the floor ahead of the vote on the data center legislation, Heinrich said "this is nothing more than a messaging bill on the eve of an election."
"Congress needs to pass a law with real teeth," he added.

articles.title_orig: Moscow threatens nuclear response over tiny fortress wedged between US allies as clash fears grow
articles.title_zh: Moscow threatens nuclear response over tiny fortress wedged between US allies as clash fears grow

Professor Azeem Ibrahim says Russia’s heavily militarized Baltic enclave has become a testing ground for hybrid warfare targeting European infrastructure.
Russia’s warning that it could resort to nuclear weapons if NATO attempts to isolate Kaliningrad is raising new concerns that the heavily militarized Russian exclave could become a flashpoint between Moscow and the alliance, as experts warn the territory is already being used to pressure Europe through hybrid warfare.
Moscow warned NATO in a diplomatic document that it was prepared to use "the entire arsenal of forces and capabilities at its disposal, including nuclear weapons" if alliance members attempted to isolate Kaliningrad from the rest of Russia, Reuters reported Wednesday.
Kaliningrad, a Russian territory geographically separated from the Russian mainland, sits on the Baltic Sea between NATO members Poland and Lithuania and hosts significant Russian military assets, including elements of Moscow’s Baltic Fleet.
RUSSIA THREATENS STRIKES ON UK MILITARY TARGETS, ‘CATASTROPHIC CONSEQUENCES’ OVER UKRAINE
Russian President Vladimir Putin looks on a map showing the Kaliningrad exclave and the rest of Russia, Sept. 10, 2006. (Konstantin Zavrazhin/Gamma-Rapho via Getty Images)
The Russian document also raised the possibility of strikes against "decision-making centers" in NATO member states from the outset of a conflict.
NATO rejected Moscow’s allegations in a response reviewed by Fox News Digital, saying the alliance is defensive and that none of its exercises or activities threaten Russian territory. The alliance also urged Russia to stop its "irresponsible nuclear rhetoric."
Carrie Filipetti, executive director of the Vandenberg Coalition, a nonpartisan network of foreign policy leaders, told Fox News Digital that Moscow has repeatedly used nuclear threats as a means of trying to deter Western support for Ukraine.
"Russia has threatened to use nuclear weapons in the past, including veiled references to tactical nuclear attacks at the beginning of Putin's invasion of Ukraine , lowering their formal threshold for launching a nuclear attack in 2024, placing Russia's nuclear forces on high alert, and restarting nuclear testing," Filipetti said. "It is very common for Putin to use these threats, because he sees it as a way to deter Europe and the United States from continuing to support Ukraine."
SHE GREW UP UNDER SOVIET RULE. NOW EU'S TOP DIPLOMAT WARNS EUROPE AGAINST GIVING RUSSIA WHAT IT WANTS
The Blue Ridge-class command and control ship USS Mount Whitney participates in exercise Baltic Operations 2025 as ships sail in formation through the Baltic Sea, June 5, 2025. (U.S. Navy Courtesy Photo)
"The threat about a nuclear attack if Kaliningrad is threatened or isolated comes on the heels of a few developments," she added, pointing to NATO jets being scrambled over Russian aircraft, U.S. and NATO air drills near Kaliningrad last month, and heightened tensions over the war in Ukraine.
Filipetti, who also served as a deputy assistant secretary at the State Department and as a senior policy advisor for the United States Mission to the United Nations (USUN), argued that the timing also reflects mounting pressure on Moscow as the war continues.
"Putin seems to understand that the tide is turning against him, and he's resorting to aggressive rhetoric to try to stop European support for Ukraine as he has tried to do in the past," she said.
Dr. Azeem Ibrahim, a research professor at the Strategic Studies Institute at the U.S. Army War College and chief strategy officer at the New Lines Institute, told Fox News Digital that NATO should take the warning seriously, particularly because of the broader role Kaliningrad is already playing in Moscow’s confrontation with Europe.
BATTLE-TESTED ZELENSKYY SOUNDS CHILLING ALARM ON WHERE PUTIN’S WAR COULD HEAD NEXT
NATO's largest annual maritime drill, Exercise Dynamic Mariner/Flotex 25, continues in the Gulf of Cadiz off southern Spain on March 28, 2025. (Burak Akbulut/Anadolu via Getty Images)
Ibrahim argued that while NATO has traditionally prepared for conventional military conflict involving "tanks and troops and divisions," Russia is increasingly using methods designed to disrupt the infrastructure and systems on which civilian societies depend.
"Russia is actually adopting a very different approach," he said, describing a strategy of hybrid warfare targeting "infrastructure" and "societies in general — what keeps societies functioning."
Ibrahim described Kaliningrad as the "front line" of that effort.
"It’s essentially become a Russian fortress," he said. "This is essentially a front-line operation of the Russians in terms of signals intelligence, signals interference and essentially mechanisms by which to carry out this hybrid warfare."
Such interference, Ibrahim said, could play a role in the broader confrontation by disrupting civilian communications and infrastructure before or alongside a conventional military attack.
"All of that would be preceded by interference operations like this to ensure that societies are not functioning, are not able to respond to emergency services, the news information services, etc.," Ibrahim said. "So governments lose control over what actually makes societies function."
RUSSIA'S SHADOW WAR IS PUTTING EUROPE ON EDGE AS GERMANY CONFRONTS A GROWING THREAT
Soldiers from Poland’s 18th Division demonstrate battlefield medical training near the Belarus border after a serviceman from the division was killed in an attack by an illegal migrant. May 16, 2026. (Efrat Lachter/Fox News Digital)
The challenge for NATO, he said, is that such operations can be more difficult to attribute than a conventional assault.
"Many times, you cannot trace exactly where a lot of this interference is actually coming from — attacks on power stations or internet and telecommunications, et cetera," Ibrahim said. "There’s always some sort of plausible deniability if it’s done by an actor who's very capable."
The ambiguity, Ibrahim argued, presents a challenge for an alliance built around collective defense against armed attack.
"NATO really does have to kind of reconfigure its posture to understand that these kinds of attacks are equivalent to essentially any sort of kinetic attack," he said.
Asked what NATO and neighboring Poland and Lithuania should do following Russia’s warning, Ibrahim called for the alliance to establish clearer consequences for hybrid attacks.
"We now need to start going on the offensive in terms of hybrid warfare and understanding the threat and pushing back and sending a very clear signal to Moscow that such threats will not stand," he said, arguing that a sufficiently serious hybrid attack should be considered capable of triggering NATO’s Article 5 collective-defense clause.
Lithuania, which directly borders Kaliningrad, rejected Moscow’s warning and accused Russia of trying to undermine NATO unity and Western support for Ukraine.
"Russia’s insinuations and threats have no basis. NATO is a defensive alliance and poses no threat to Russia or any other country," Lithuania’s Foreign Ministry told Fox News Digital. "Russia’s threatening is intended to fracture transatlantic unity and impede our support to Ukraine. Russia will not achieve its goals."
The ministry added: "We strongly condemn any threats to use force and irresponsible nuclear rhetoric. Russia must stop its aggression against Ukraine… Lithuania is strengthening its national defense system and capabilities, including air defense," the ministry said. "We train with our allies and work alongside NATO forces deployed in Lithuania. We are prepared to defend every inch of NATO territory and respond to any threats."
The ministry said Lithuania would also continue providing "comprehensive support to Ukraine and its fight against the aggressor Russia."

articles.content_orig:
WASHINGTON — Senate Democrats blocked legislation Wednesday aimed at protecting consumers from paying higher prices when new data centers are built in their communities.
The vote was 57-43, short of the 60 needed to break a filibuster.
The Ratepayer Protection Act , which passed the House by a vote of 417-3 two weeks ago, sets a federal standard on the issue. It also instructs state public utility commissions to find ways to make developers of data centers that use huge amounts of energy cover their own costs of water and electricity to consumers.
The Senate version is led by appointed Sen. Jon Husted, R-Ohio, who’s locked in a competitive battle as he seeks his first full Senate term. He’s facing heat at home from Democratic rival and former senator Sherrod Brown, who has branded him “the face of data centers” for promoting developments when he was lieutenant governor.
“I heard they said they wanted lower electricity prices,” Husted said of Democrats on Tuesday. “All they have to do is not block it, vote for it, and it will be on the president’s desk, and we will have a bipartisan win.”
Senate Minority Leader Chuck Schumer, D-N.Y., said the bill is merely “optional” for states and won’t achieve much beyond partisan messaging for Republicans.
“Plain and simple, the Ratepayer Protection Act is a fraud,” Schumer told reporters on Tuesday. “It does not require any protections at all. While Americans are demanding real guardrails on AI and data centers, Republicans are offering a toothless messaging bill. We need real action on data centers.”
Schumer said Republicans should instead take up bills by Sens. Chris Van Hollen , D-Md., and Martin Heinrich , D-N.M., that would go further in imposing cost-related rules on data centers.
Senate Majority Leader John Thune, R-S.D., rejected Democratic arguments that the bill is simply a Republican political move to protect Husted’s re-election bid. He noted that nearly every House Democrat voted for the measure.
“I don’t know how you can say something that passed the House of Representatives 417-3 isn’t consequential,” Thune told reporters. “AOC voted for it over there. Hakeem Jeffries voted for it over there. This is a bill that could go to the president and become law. Evidently, a lot of Democrats in the House of Representatives thought it was important to be for and thought that it did exactly what the bill says it does.”
An NBC News poll this month found that data centers are unpopular: By nearly 6 to 1, voters said they’d be less likely to vote for a candidate who supports building a data center in their community. The survey found that voters trust Democrats over Republicans by a margin of 12 points to deal with data centers.
Sen. Thom Tillis, R-N.C., who is retiring, said Husted was “right to get the message out” on data center costs.
But when asked if the bill would achieve much beyond that, Tillis said, “No.”
“I think the best way to deal with this is ... down in North Carolina, most utilities are managed through public utility commissions,” Tillis said. “They’re managed through local and state decision-making. That’s where it should be.”

articles.content_orig:
By DAVID BARRETT, HOME AFFAIRS EDITOR
Published: 12:01 EDT, 30 September 2026 | Updated: 14:20 EDT, 30 September 2026
Labour's 'one in, one out' migrant deal with France has been scrapped just over a year after it came into operation.
The Home Office announced the scheme – which allowed Channel small boat migrants to be returned to France – was 'no longer processing new cases'.
Its failure will be a blow to Labour's attempts to tackle the Channel crisis, and could risk an up-tick in small boat arrivals after recent falls.
Cases that are already in the system will continue, the Home Office said, including bringing migrants to Britain from France if they are accepted under the reciprocal terms of the deal.
The first removal under the scheme took place on September 18 last year.
In all, more than 1,500 migrants have been returned to France and 'just under' 1,500 have come to the UK, it is understood.
A Home Office spokesman said: 'We continue to work with France to relentlessly tackle small boat crossings , and we've made real progress.
'Numbers are significantly down on last year and crossings this summer were the lowest in six years.
Migrants try to board a smuggler's boat off the beach of Equihen-Plage, northern France, last week
'The government's pilot with France to remove asylum seekers in exchange for an equal number of legal migrants is no longer processing new cases.
'However, flights will continue over the coming weeks to swiftly remove small boat migrants from the UK, and we will use lessons learned from the pilot to accelerate efforts to return small boat migrants with no right to remain in the UK.'
Shadow Home Secretary Chris Philp said: 'This is another borders humiliation for the Labour government.
'First their laughable promise to smash the gangs disintegrated.
'Then the plans to get the French to stops boats launching in shallow water fell apart.
'With 95 per cent of illegal Channel migrants allowed to stay in the UK, no wonder almost 20,000 have crossed so far this year with over 1,000 arriving last week alone.
' Only when all illegal immigrants are deported within a week of arrival will the crossings finally stop - which the Conservative borders plan will do.'
Labour scrapped the Conservatives' Rwanda asylum deal as one of its first acts in office in 2024.
Instead, the Government has insisted it can tackle the Channel crisis by increasing law enforcement activities both here and in Europe, along with closer co-operation with the French.
There had been an expectation that the 'one in, one out' deal would be extended - at least until the end of this month and possibly longer.
But the French have instead voiced their aspiration for a wider deal which would see Britain accepting migrants not only from France but from other parts of the European Union too.
Earlier this month Home Secretary Shabana Mahmood said the cost of sending small boat migrants back to France under the deal had risen to £56,000 a head.
Previous figures had put the cost of each return at less than £50,000.
She also told MPs 'relatively small' numbers of migrants had been involved in the scheme and it had been 'operationally difficult to scale up very large numbers of removals every week into the French system'.
The collapse of the French deal comes after last week witnessed chaos on the Channel with two dinghies reaching the Kent coast without being intercepted by UK Border Force.
It also saw an unprecedented 38-hour voyage from Normandy by a small boat, raising fresh questions over the efficacy of Labour's beach patrol agreement with the French, which carries a £662million price tag for the British taxpayer.

'When you get to this stage in your life, you begin to unpack what’s yours and what’s always sort of been for everyone else,' Bush told Vogue of their decision to keep their marriage a secret.
