articles.title_orig: MI5 warns UK academics to cut ties with Chinese group over alleged spying
articles.title_zh: MI5 warns UK academics to cut ties with Chinese group over alleged spying
articles.content_orig:
Britain’s domestic intelligence agency has told academics to stop working with a Chinese organisation funding research in United Kingdom universities, accusing it of having “very strong ties” with China’s spy agency.
In a rare public espionage alert on Wednesday, MI5 alleged the ⁠⁠”primary purpose” of the China General Technology Research Institute (CGTRI) is to finance academic work that improves the espionage capability of the Ministry of State Security (MSS), the Chinese intelligence agency.
There was no immediate response from Beijing, which has previously strongly denied such accusations.
MI5 said the CGTRI targeted more than 100 UK-based academics working in areas such as artificial intelligence, cybersecurity, covert communications systems and steganography.
It said many academics and institutions would have engaged in good faith with the organisation, unaware of its close ties to the MSS. But it added those who continued to take grants from or work with the CGTRI now risked prosecution under the UK’s National Security Act, a law passed in 2023 that gave the government greater powers to target foreign espionage and hostile state activities.
“This activity supports MSS espionage, which poses a threat to UK national security,” MI5 said.
UK Security Minister ⁠⁠Dan Jarvis said he had written to all university leaders in Britain to ensure staff ended any relationship with the CGTRI.
“This alert exposes attempts by Chinese intelligence to covertly benefit from the expertise and research of our academics, undermining our national security, and that of our allies,” he said in a statement.
“International ⁠⁠partnerships are vital to ensure our universities and research institutes continue to thrive, but we will take robust action to defend against the threats we face.”
The UK’s relationship with China, its third largest trading partner, has become ⁠⁠increasingly complex in recent years.
The government in London has sought ⁠⁠better relations with Beijing to improve trade ties and earlier this year approved plans for China to build its largest embassy in Europe in the UK capital. But it has also repeatedly warned of Chinese spying efforts and attempts to undermine the UK’s democratic system.
Last year, Ken McCallum, MI5’s director-general, said Chinese spies were creating fake job adverts to try to dupe British professionals into handing over data.
His agency also issued an alert to UK lawmakers last November that Chinese agents were targeting them to collect information and influence their activity by posing as headhunters or companies.
In ‌‌June, ‌‌security agencies from the Five Eyes intelligence alliance – the US, Britain, Canada, Australia and New Zealand – published a warning about Chinese spies aggressively using online job platforms to recruit people with access to sensitive information.
China’s London embassy said the warning was “entirely fabricated and constitutes malicious slander”.

articles.title_orig: Court Pauses Execution of Tennessee’s Lone Woman on Death Row
articles.title_zh: Court Pauses Execution of Tennessee’s Lone Woman on Death Row
articles.content_orig:
A federal appeals court has temporarily stopped Tennessee from executing death row inmate Christa Pike , intervening less than two hours before she was due to receive a lethal injection.
The 6th US Circuit Court of Appeals granted what it called a “short stay of execution” on Wednesday while judges consider Pike’s argument that evidence of sexual abuse she experienced as a child was not properly weighed when she was sentenced.
Tennessee officials quickly turned to the US Supreme Court, asking the justices to lift the stay and allow the execution to proceed.
Pike, 50, had been scheduled to die at Riverbend Maximum Security Institution in Nashville. Had the execution gone ahead, she would have been the first woman executed by Tennessee in more than two centuries.
She was sentenced to death for the 1995 killing of Colleen Slemmer, a 19-year-old classmate at a Knoxville vocational centre.
Pike was 18 when she, her 17-year-old boyfriend Tadaryl Shipp, and another teenager tortured and killed Slemmer. Pike and Shipp were later convicted of first-degree murder. Shipp received a life sentence with the possibility of parole.
Pike’s lawyers have argued that her childhood was marked by violence, neglect and sexual abuse, including rapes when she was 11 and 17 years old. They also cited her later diagnoses of bipolar disorder and post-traumatic stress disorder in seeking to have her sentence reduced to life without parole.
Tennessee Governor Bill Lee rejected that clemency request. Slemmer’s mother, May Martinez, has publicly supported the execution.
The case has also attracted international scrutiny, with a group of United Nations human rights experts calling for Pike’s death sentence to be commuted.
Women have accounted for just 18 of the 1,683 executions carried out in the US since capital punishment resumed in 1976. Pike’s case is more unusual still: If the execution ultimately proceeds, she would be the only person in Tennessee’s modern death penalty era put to death for a crime committed as a teenager.

articles.content_orig:
On morning service from Dubai to Tel Aviv, 150 passengers witnessed a horrific cockpit assault and a daring rescue
Pilot who stabbed co-pilot on Israel-bound plane may have tried to crash it, says Netanyahu
A s flight FZ 1073 soared west over the waters of the Gulf towards Israel , its passengers may have bemoaned a 20-minute delay at takeoff. For a low-cost airline route, flydubai’s daily service to Tel Aviv is usually convenient and reliable. The nonstop flight takes about three and a half hours and departs early enough from Dubai that it usually lands at Ben Gurion airport at about 9am local time.
That was not the case for Wednesday’s catastrophic flight. The passenger jet never made it to its scheduled destination. Instead, it dropped thousands of feet in seconds before limping down to make an emergency landing in Saudi Arabia – perhaps miraculously, since photos suggested a large part of the tail of the aircraft was missing.
Passengers evacuated, some covered in blood, with stories to share of a pilot-on-pilot stabbing, and footage posted online from inside the fuselage showed the aftermath of violence.
In one video, two men lie on the floor with breathing masks on their faces as passengers stand over them in the cramped gangway. One wears a white shirt soaked red with blood, and the distinctive pilot stripes on his shoulders. He appears almost unresponsive. The other man blinks slowly, with blood smeared on the wall next to him. A person off camera appears to encourage the injured man to remain conscious: “No sleep,” he says.
More footage, apparently from a seat further back, shows passengers screaming and weeping in distress as the Boeing 737 Max shakes. Israeli media reported that the plane was carrying about 150 Israeli passengers.
Accounts from the airline, passenger testimony, flight trackers and Israeli officials describe a series of horrific events starting about two and a half hours after takeoff.
The flight tracking website Flightradar24 recorded the aircraft abruptly descending from its cruising altitude of about 34,000ft to 17,000ft in less than two minutes. Investigators will look at whether such a sudden and ferocious movement was the reason for damage to the aircraft’s rudder.
Minutes later, the plane sent out a series of emergency transponder signals in the form of “squawk codes”. These four-digit codes are normally used by pilots to broadcast their position but can be used in an emergency situation, even if pilots are in radio contact with air traffic control.
Aircraft trackers at Flightradar24 said the flydubai plane transmitted emergency and hijack signals. The aircraft made an erratic circle close to the Jordanian border before turning around and heading south.
In one video, a passenger with blood dripping from an open wound on his head pleads for assistance and says the jet is descending into Saudi Arabia. “Whoever is hearing me, we need help,” the man says in Hebrew. “We are in the Tabuk area of Saudi Arabia, which we don’t know. All the passengers are OK except for the pilot. We need help.”
What was happening during these critical minutes is still being investigated, but early unconfirmed reports pointed to a cockpit fight, followed by passengers storming up the aisle, and then either one or more pilots who were travelling as passengers wresting control of the plane to avert a disaster.
The Israeli newspaper Haaretz cited a passenger as saying that the plane lost control and began to dive.
Dalia Shpigel was quoted as saying that “suddenly there were terrible screams throughout the plane” before “three to five guys burst into the cockpit” and subdued the alleged assailant and began treating an injured pilot.
“We realised that the situation was stabilising and continued the flight. Gradually, information began to emerge about what had happened in the cockpit,” Shpigel told Haaretz.
Her fellow passenger Miryam Shira Ohayon said the “co-pilot tried to murder the pilot and basically carry out a suicide attack on the plane”.
Speaking to reporters via speakerphone held up by her mother, who was waiting at Ben Gurion airport, she said the plane “was really on the way to crashing, and it was simply the resourcefulness of many people who took control of the co-pilot and neutralised him”.
“There was also a doctor who gave first aid, and people who treated both of them … but the bigger fear was really a crash, which is exactly what he was trying to do,” she said.
The Emirati carrier, in a statement later on Wednesday, said the aircraft was “successfully secured by on-duty flydubai crew travelling on the flight”, who diverted and landed the aircraft safely at Tabuk airport. Airlines often move pilots around different airports as passengers, and it is possible it was these pilots who sent the emergency codes.
One passenger, Almog Itali, was quoted by the BBC as saying that one of the pilots onboard who stabilised the plane was British. “There were two spare pilots who were supposed to operate the next flight,” he said. “The relief pilots are European, one of them British, who entered [the cockpit] and pulled the aircraft up, pulled the yoke, stabilised the plane and landed us in Saudi Arabia.”
Stanislav Bukhman, the head of risk at Osprey Flight Solutions, an aviation security firm based in the UK, said investigators were likely to focus on a few key areas, including how pilots were vetted, and crew screening at the departure airport.
On how the flight deck might have been accessed, he said cabin crew could request entry to the cockpit using an emergency access code. “This exists for situations where the pilots are incapacitated. There is a safeguard built in, though. If the pilots are conscious and operating normally, they can deny that request and keep the door locked. This is designed to protect the flight deck in a hijacking or hostage situation,” he said.
“At this stage there isn’t enough information to say how the flight deck on FZ 1073 was accessed. The door may have been opened by the captain, who reportedly resisted the co-pilot’s attempt to take control, or by cabin crew using the emergency procedure.”
The Israeli prime minister, Benjamin Netanyahu, announced that one of the pilots had planned to crash and kill its mostly Israeli passengers, who stopped a “major disaster” with their actions. The alleged assailant was arrested after the plane landed, Netanyahu ‌said.
“During the flight, as they approached the country, one of the pilots stabbed the other pilot and apparently tried to crash the plane with everyone onboard,” Netanyahu said in a video message, calling the passengers “heroes”. All the passengers were accounted for and safe.
Flydubai, however, said an “altercation” occurred in the flight deck of flight FZ 1073, and it warned against drawing conclusions about the motive.
“At this early stage, the underlying reasons and motives behind this event are unknown and remain subject to a formal investigation,” a flydubai spokesperson said in a statement. “We urge all parties to refrain from premature speculation while authorities gather the facts.”

American troops are scheduled to exit their final military posts in Iraq on Wednesday, a pullout welcomed as a triumph by Iran and its partners. Their sway runs deep across the country, where over two decades of fighting claimed 4,500 U.S. lives.
Nevertheless, the United States has retained practical power over Iraq's oil revenue since its 2003 invasion. That financial leverage grants Washington immense control over affairs in Baghdad, carrying significant implications for regional dynamics involving Iran.
At the center of the issue is how the Federal Reserve Bank of New York handles Iraq's oil earnings.
Following the 2003 military campaign, the American-led Coalition Provisional Authority (CPA) created the Development Fund for Iraq (DFI). Housed at the New York Fed, this mechanism was established to gather energy income intended for national rebuilding and redevelopment projects.
The initiative was also structured to safeguard these assets from legal actions and claims originating from Saddam Hussein's regime.
Formed under an executive directive from then-President George W. Bush, the system has been extended by every president since. The DFI was ultimately converted into a Central Bank of Iraq account at the New York Federal Reserve, where it continues to operate.
Generating roughly 90 percent of its total state budget, crude oil is Iraq's primary economic resource, giving Washington considerable influence over the nation's political and financial stability.
When Iraqi leaders requested the withdrawal of American forces in 2020, Washington reportedly threatened to block access to Baghdad's New York Federal Reserve accounts, forcing the government to back down.
Although Iraq has gained greater authority over its financial matters since the initial occupation years, this connection underscores the US's lasting influence on the Iraqi economy, even as the country tries to assert full political independence and national sovereignty.
Iraq's financial stability has been secured by the mechanism, which protects public funds, government sources told Reuters anonymously.
According to officials, the framework strengthens international trust in oil revenue oversight, facilitates access to American currency required for commercial trade and imports, and shields state income from external legal claims, creditor demands, and broader economic shocks.
The setup stabilizes exchange rates and reinforces faith in the national economy, helping fortify local financial institutions while asserting broader economic control, officials added.
It also gives the government leverage to push back against factions, including Iran-backed groups, that demand fewer restrictions on dollar access. Last year, the U.S. targeted several Iraqi banks and figures with sanctions over allegations of money laundering for Tehran.
Heavy curbs on U.S. dollar supply led to a parallel, informal market for dollars, creating a price spread between the central bank's official exchange rate and the black-market rate. The ​price difference is essentially a risk premium for dealing outside the formal system. In his second term,
​Trump has pursued a ⁠campaign of maximum pressure on Iran , with Iraq often caught in the crossfire as Tehran has used it as a vital economic lung. The war he launched with Israel against Iran on February 28 added further pressure on Baghdad.
The Federal Reserve Bank of New York continues to hold custody of Iraq's oil earnings.
To supply American dollars, the CBI traditionally relied on dollar auctions, officially known as the foreign currency window. This allowed private banks and exchange firms to bid daily for U.S. currency using Iraqi dinars.
Under heavy U.S. pressure, Iraq officially shuttered this auction framework in early 2025, driven by a broader crackdown targeting the alleged siphoning of dollars to sanctioned parties, particularly Iran.

articles.title_orig: Romania’s political crisis intensifies as Parliament rejects pro-EU PM
articles.title_zh: Romania’s political crisis intensifies as Parliament rejects pro-EU PM
articles.content_orig:
Romania’s pro-European Prime Minister-designate Siegfried Muresan has failed to win a parliamentary vote of confidence, prolonging a political crisis seen as a boost for the rising far right.
Muresan, a liberal European Parliament member who was the latest of three designated prime ministers, secured only 182 votes out of the 233 required to secure the confidence motion on Wednesday, according to the official count.
The far-right Alliance for the Union of Romanians (AUR) largely boycotted the vote.
The 45-year-old had proposed what he described as a “reform-oriented” governing programme under his centre-right National Liberal Party (PNL), which teamed up with the Save Romania Union party, or USR, and the small ethnic Hungarian UDMR party.
President Nicusor Dan said he would nominate a new prime minister candidate on Monday afternoon, after holding talks with the leaders of the parliamentary parties, to avoid snap elections.
Romania saw the collapse of a pro-European coalition government in May, when governing social democrats, together with the opposition far right, ousted liberal Prime Minister Ilie Bolojan in a no-confidence motion at that time.
The far right, which comprises about a third of Parliament, threatened to impeach the president if he does not call early elections once the conditions are met.
Romania, a member of the EU and NATO that borders Ukraine, has not held snap elections since the fall of communism in 1989.
Political analyst Cristian Pirvulescu told the AFP news agency that snap elections would lead to another fragmented Parliament, but with an emboldened far right.
“Early elections mean that, from the moment they are called, it would take four months before a new government could be formed,” Pirvulescu told AFP. “Due to political instability, Romania finds itself in a very complicated economic situation. Four months is already a very long time.”
The country of 19 million has been struggling for months with the highest public deficit and inflation in the European Union.

Xbox CEO Asha Sharma is taking a ‘long-term view’ of Microsoft’s gaming division.
Xbox CEO Asha Sharma is taking a ‘long-term view’ of Microsoft’s gaming division.
Xbox CEO Asha Sharma has denied reports that Microsoft is considering selling off its Xbox business. The Information reported in June that Microsoft CEO Satya Nadella and CFO Amy Hood had been considering spinning out Xbox entirely, and then reported earlier this month that both execs have “more recently supported Sharma’s plans to overhaul the unit.”
“Xbox is not for sale,” says Sharma in an interview with The New York Times . “We will do whatever it takes to set the company up for success, and we will look at the right partnerships, the right operating model and everything needed to achieve that.”
It appears that Nadella and Hood have favored the giant Xbox “reset” as the plan for Microsoft’s gaming unit instead of making Xbox a joint venture or spinning out the gaming business entirely. Sharma announced her Xbox restructuring in June, calling it a reset for the division. Microsoft is planning to lay off up to 3,200 Xbox employees over the course of its 2027 financial year, which ends in June.
Nadella backed Sharma’s restructuring and layoffs in a recent appearance on the Sources podcast . “There’s some amount of streamlining the team is doing, and Asha is doing, which is great to see,” said Nadella last week. “And then we have to invent the right sustainable business model that allows us to deliver gaming to more and more people.”
The most recent restructuring has seen Halo move under Activision, as well as the developers behind Sea of Thieves and Age of Empires . Alongside a major shake-up of Xbox Game Studios, the recent changes look geared toward making Xbox a wholly owned subsidiary like Microsoft does with LinkedIn.
Microsoft is reducing management layers at Xbox, offloading smaller studios, and focusing on its larger Xbox franchises. That could eventually end in an Xbox sale at some point in the future, but right now the plan seems to be about bringing growth back to Xbox. “We’ve got a long way to go with Microsoft,” says Sharma, “and we’re going to take the long-term view.”
But as Sharma said in February , “The plan’s the plan until it’s not the plan.”

articles.title_zh: Trump administration starts sending $500 Obamacare refund checks — who stands to benefit
articles.content_orig:
The Trump administration said it will start sending refund checks on Wednesday to Affordable Care Act enrollees across the U.S. who it says were "overcharged" by the Biden administration.
Nearly 1 million Americans across 30 states will receive the $500 checks, along with a letter from President Trump.
"For years, the Biden Administration overcharged you to fund the operation of HealthCare.gov," Mr. Trump says in the letter, a copy of which was shared with CBS News. "That money belongs to hard-working Americans, not the Government, and now, I am returning it to you!"
Some families with more than one "affected person" could receive multiple payments via check or direct deposit, an administration official told CBS News. The primary recipients of the checks will be people who earn above 400% of the federal poverty line, the official added.
The states where people are getting refunds rely on federal exchanges administered by the Centers for Medicare and Medicaid Services, which charges a user fee. The White House said earlier this month that it is issuing the refunds because the Biden administration overcharged Americans through those fees and then passed it on to consumers in the form of higher premium costs — what it referred to as a "gross mismanagement of Obamacare."
"With this Historic Action, my Administration is taking the surplus funds that accumulated from the ObamacarePremium Taxand issuing a one-time $500 REFUND to Americans who use the HealthCare.gov platform to purchase their health insurance, but who do not receive Taxpayer Subsidies to pay for their Coverage," the president said in his letter.
Millions of Obamacare recipients are facing higher premiums after Congress last year allowed coverage subsidies to expire. In a KFF poll released in March, half of the respondents said their premiums, deductibles or other costs are "a lot higher" than they were last year.
The Trump administration's refund effort comes with just over a month to go until the midterm elections and as affordability concerns are weighing on many households. High inflation and gas prices due to the war with Iran have pushed the president's approval ratings on the economy to near-record lows.

articles.title_orig: DOJ ramps up fight against federal judges after some in Minnesota speak to media about immigration surge cases
articles.title_zh: DOJ ramps up fight against federal judges after some in Minnesota speak to media about immigration surge cases
articles.content_orig:
Washington — The Justice Department took the unusual step on Wednesday of filing a judicial misconduct complaint against all but one of the federal district judges in Minnesota, after most of them spoke with the New York Times about concerns over the government's handling of cases during its surge in immigration enforcement earlier this year.
Attorney General Todd Blanche announced the filing of the complaint with the U.S. Court of Appeals for the 8th Circuit at a press conference, where he also said that prosecutors in Minnesota had secured an indictment against 10 noncitizens for allegedly casting votes unlawfully in prior elections.
"We have a right, just like every litigant in court, to have a judge that will be fair and impartial," Blanche said. "We have no choice but to act."
At the heart of the complaint is a New York Times story published earlier this month headlined "Trump's Minnesota Surge Threatened Democracy, Judge Warns." As a part of the story, Judge Patrick Schiltz sat for a 90-minute interview and shared his views on what he said were repeated violations of court orders by the Trump administration. The article said that six of the seven members of Minnesota's federal bench also spoke with reporters to discuss the federal government's immigration crackdown in the state, called Operation Metro Surge.
Schiltz was appointed to the federal bench by President George W. Bush and clerked for Justice Antonin Scalia on the Supreme Court.
The judicial misconduct complaint names Schiltz and Judge John Tunheim, appointed by President Bill Clinton, as well as "anonymous district judges" serving on the U.S. District Court for the District of Minnesota. In the article, Tunheim pushed back on the Trump administration's claim that it was arresting the "worst of the worst" in Minnesota.
"They weren't arresting, in my view, people who were dangerous criminals on the street," Tunheim told the Times.
The Justice Department said Schiltz and Tunheim's conduct "is particularly egregious" and claimed the two "flagrantly violated the Code of Judicial Conduct with their improper and unethical comments" to the Times.
The complaint is signed by Acting Deputy Attorney General Trent McCotter and Associate Attorney General Stanley Woodward.
The officials said Schiltz's comments in particular were "overly political and concern matters that are pending," either before the judge or an appeals court. They said that Tunheim's comment was "less verbose" but "equally unethical."
"If anything is a 'grave threat to the rule of law,' it is judges who repeatedly and brazenly exceed their authority then launch a partisan press campaign that includes criticizing the government for filing an emergency appeal when a judge refused to rule on a search warrant application," McCotter and Woodward wrote.
They asked the 8th Circuit to order Schiltz and Tunheim to recuse themselves from matters involving the Department of Homeland Security. They said the appeals court should also launch an investigation into the "improper conduct" of Minnesota judges who "'covet publicity' rather than adhering to the rule of law by adjudicating cases or controversies."
The Trump administration launched Operation Metro Surge in December 2025 and deployed more than 3,000 immigration authorities to Minnesota as part of its immigration enforcement campaign. Border czar Tom Homan announced in February that Operation Metro Surge would be coming to an end and there would be a drawdown of federal immigration officers in the state.
But the stepped-up immigration actions led to violent clashes between federal authorities and protesters. Two people, Renee Good and Alex Pretti , were killed in Minnesota in January, sparking criticism of the tactics used by Immigration and Customs Enforcement and Customs and Border Protection.
In the federal courts, judges in Minnesota were inundated with scores of petitions from migrants challenging their detentions and asking to be freed. In a pair of extraordinary orders issued in the case of an Ecuadorian man, Schiltz accused the Trump administration of failing to respond to "dozens" of court orders. He identified 96 court orders in 74 cases that he said ICE had violated.
"ICE is not a law unto itself," he wrote in one order issued Jan. 28.
In another, from two days earlier, Schiltz said the Trump administration "decided to send thousands of agents to Minnesota to detain aliens without making any provision for dealing with the hundreds of habeas petitions and other lawsuits that were sure to result" and said "the court's patience is at an end."

The idea for what became President Donald Trumpâs Tuesday pact with the AI industry came from a conversation between Meta CEO Mark Zuckerberg and House Speaker Mike Johnson at last weekâs state dinner, a source familiar with the matter told Semafor.
Zuckerberg spoke to Johnson â whom he was seated next to at the dinner for Chinese leader Xi Jinping â about regulatory concerns around AI, according to the source. The Meta CEO then talked to Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang about crafting a set of principles that tech executives could use at their next meeting with Trump, the source added.
Zuckerberg then circulated a draft ahead of Tuesdayâs meeting between Trump and AI executives. Huang played a role gathering support for it among the administrationâs guests, which included executives from OpenAI, Anthropic, xAI, and others. Eventually Trump himself released the document as a âWhite House Accord on Super Intelligence,â outlining broad principles for self-regulation.
The Trump administration and the industry executives who gathered on Tuesday hailed it as a historic concord among rival companies that signaled the industry wants to act responsibly, though itâs not clear that the gesture will quell broad public concerns about safety.
Zuckerbergâs central role in shaping the document, confirmed by two other sources familiar with the matter, indicates that his cultivation of Trump has paid off. It also suggests that his political clout can rival that of the free-spending Musk and Huang â who recently made headlines by speaking to the president onstage at an industry conference.
Meta did not comment for this story. The White House did not return a request for comment.
The accord, signed by Meta, OpenAI, Anthropic, xAI, Google, and NVIDIA, lays out a commitment to ârobust internal controlsâ and outside audits designed to ensure the safety of frontier AI models. Some of those models abide by a voluntary clearance by the government under a framework established by a Trump order on AI, though that framework was never released to the public.
At just over 300 words, the agreement doesnât get into significant detail about what those industry-run safety controls might look like in practice. The agreement also hints that federal AI regulation may be needed in the future.
Zuckerberg described it as âgood steps forwardâ on Tuesday.
âThe idea isnât that this is the only thing that we will ever do. It is that this is a start and an accord that the whole industry could come to,â Zuckerberg told reporters outside the White House Tuesday, appearing next to Trump, House Speaker Mike Johnson and others who attended the meeting.
Zuckerberg survived the âtechlashâ relatively unscathed in Washington following the 2016 presidential election, only after years of being yelled at by both parties in Congress. He testified multiple times on everything from election interference via Facebook ads to kidsâ online safety, along with playing key roles in battles over privacy and content moderation. Meta later faced a lot of litigation, from both the federal government and private actors. The company dealt with the brunt of Big Tech animosity before AI companies ever even had offices in Washington. Things have shifted now. Metaâs even been forgiven by the right for kicking Trump off the platform following the Capitol riot. With the benefit of hindsight and experience, Zuckerberg knows how to skate where the puck is going politically; heâs trying to position Meta as willing to work with the government and disinterested in excessive regulation. Itâs a strategy thatâs working â with this president.

Carnegie Mellon University just received a historic $3 billion donation from Citadel CEO Ken Griffin.
Carnegie Mellon, which is located in Pittsburgh , announced the gift Wednesday morning. The university says it intends to use $2 billion to open a new campus in Miami , called Carnegie Mellon University Miami.
“We are deeply grateful to Ken Griffin for his extraordinary vision, partnership and belief in what Carnegie Mellon can achieve,” CMU President Farnam Jahanian said in a statement.
Construction is scheduled to begin in 2027 and should be open to new students in 2028, presuming there are no major regulatory hurdles, according to the Pittsburgh Post-Gazette .
Griffin bought the 35 acres in Wynwood, Florida, where the university will be built, for $1.1 billion from real estate developer Moishe Mana.
Mana said that the sale is the largest land assemblage deal in Florida history.
The campus is expected to support more than 3,500 undergraduate, master's and PhD students, plus approximately 300 faculty members and more than 600 staff.
The university said in a statement that the new school will focus its education on confronting “societal challenges” rather than on traditional academic majors.
The statement said it will focus on “challenge areas spanning human health and biological discovery; national security and strategic capabilities; energy and climate resilience; and advanced manufacturing and industrial transformation.”
The university reportedly had to “rethink” how it operates to respond to the rise of AI.
“Artificial intelligence represents one of the defining intellectual developments of our time, and it demands that we rethink how we educate students, conduct research and partner with others,” Jahanian said.
The final $1 billion of the donation will go to support Carnegie Mellon's Pittsburgh campus. Approximately half will be used to boost the university's highest priority needs, and another half will be invested in its School of Computer Science, which will be renamed the Kenneth C. Griffin School of Computer Science in his honor.
CMU said that the donation is the largest individual donor gift ever given to a university. Before Griffin’s gift, the largest individual donation to a university was Michael Bloomberg’s $1.8 billion donation to Johns Hopkins University in 2018.
This isn’t Griffin’s first investment in South Florida. He attended high school in the region, and moved Citadel’s headquarters from Chicago to Miami in 2022. He explained the move at the time by insisting that Florida had a better corporate environment than Illinois.
He said earlier this year he planned to give fewer resources to Citadel’s presence in New York and more to its efforts in South Florida. He made that decision following a public spat with New York Mayor Zohran Mamdani over a wealth tax in April.
While discussing his proposed tax in April, Mamdani called out Griffin directly, noting that he maintained a $238 million penthouse in the city while others were struggling to find homes due to a lack of affordable housing.
“We went to Miami and revised our building plan to make it a bigger office building,” Griffin said in May. “What the mayor of New York has made clear to my partners, and principally my New York partners, is that we need to double down on our bet in Miami.”

articles.title_zh: Inside the Ukrainian military unit training fighters from China
articles.content_orig:
Despite the risks, a number of soldiers from the country seen as Russia’s biggest backer have found their way to Ukraine
O n the makeshift workbench in the cramped front room of a cottage near the frontlines of the Russia-Ukraine war, there are all the accoutrements of a drone workshop . The walls are lined with pliers and rolls of duct tape; the table is cluttered with screwdrivers and piles of wire. Propped up against the wall are two kamikaze drones. Only one item looks out of place in this Ukrainian village house: a pot of Chinese longjing tea, the leaves wilted from repeated top-ups.
Good tea is one of the many things that Tim misses about his life in China. His parents post monthly supplies to Ukraine . “I think about all of it,” the 44-year-old said, of his home country. “It brings back memories and emotions.”
Tim’s teapot at the drone workshop
Tim, who asked to be referred to by his English name, is the lead volunteer in a Ukrainian military unit that this year launched an unusual project: to recruit soldiers from the country seen as Russia’s biggest backer, China .
Many Ukrainian military units have their own brands and public presences as they compete with each other for funding and new recruits. But in this case, the commander of the unit, which focuses on reconnaissance, asked that its identity be withheld because of the sensitivity of the Chinese volunteers project.
“It’s for their sake first and foremost,” said the commander, known by the call sign Muse. “For their own safety and that of their families.”
Muse said five Chinese men who had joined his unit had returned to China after completing their training because of pressure from the Chinese authorities. “We’d put our heart and soul into them,” he lamented. He is fearful that more Chinese soldiers – there are about a dozen so far in the unit – could quit if their identity is revealed. He asked that none of his soldiers’ faces be shown in photographs.
Ukraine’s military is facing an acute manpower shortage . Most of those willing to volunteer to fight have done so, and are fatigued, while some civilian men have gone into hiding to avoid being mobilised. That has turned attention to another pool of potential recruits: foreigners .
Memorial to Peng Chenliang, a Chinese soldier killed in action, fighting for Ukraine
Part of the memorial for fallen soldiers, dedicated to Chinese volunteers
There are about 16,000 foreign fighters in Ukraine, making up less than 3% of the armed forces. Before being sacked as defence minister in July, Mykhailo Fedorov passed several reforms designed to make foreign recruitment easier. He predicted that 50% of frontline service members or assault troops could be foreign citizens.
But Chinese volunteers present a unique challenge.
On the one hand, they are uniquely vulnerable to pressure from their own government. The Chinese authorities keep close tabs on their citizens. Chinese law does not specifically forbid citizens from joining foreign armies, but several Chinese volunteers in Ukraine said security services had questioned them or their relatives about their work.
A spokesperson for China’s foreign ministry said it had issued multiple security alerts “to ask Chinese nationals to stay away from areas of armed conflict … and, in particular, avoid participation in any party’s military operations”.
On the other hand, the Chinese soldiers hail from a country that has provided overwhelming support for Russia during the war in Ukraine. Although China claims to be neutral, Beijing has increased trade links with Moscow to record levels since 2022 and provided diplomatic support on numerous occasions. There have also been reports, denied by China, of high-level military cooperation between the two countries.
Roads covered with anti-drone nets in Sumy region
Some people worry that the Chinese soldiers in Ukraine could provide useful military intelligence to Beijing. An officer from another brigade said he would “think twice” before taking someone from China.
Muse, however, is unbothered. “In this situation, for us commanders, for the Ukrainian people, anyone will do. Because there aren’t enough people,” he said.
Tim, one of the Chinese volunteers, at his drone workshop
Plus, he added, the Chinese work hard. Tim’s main job in the unit is repairing drones. In one week he repaired about 10 Mavics and 15 first-person view (FPV) drones. Impressed, Muse joked that “it is better to have one Chinese person than 10 Ukrainians”.
Chinese volunteers find their way to Muse’s unit through social media and word of mouth. Although there are cursory background checks done by central authorities in Kyiv, Muse entrusts Tim to do the main screening, through a series of interviews.
Tim said the main qualities he looked for were a commitment to Ukraine’s democracy and sovereignty and an ability to communicate well. He added: “I am firmly against accepting someone who is driven simply by hatred for his own country.” He said he had already rejected more than 30 Chinese applicants since joining the unit himself in January, and that he attempted to screen out people with criminal records as well.
But in the murky world of foreign fighters, where people come with stories and claims that are often impossible to verify, dissatisfaction with one’s own country is often a factor.
Vanya, one of Chinese volunteer soldiers
Vanya, a 36-year-old from central China’s Hubei province, joined the unit over the summer.
Sitting under a trellis of grapevines outside a cottage near the frontlines, stalked by Russian FPV drones, he said life in China had become “suffocating”.
Using a VPN to jump over China’s firewall of internet censorship, he had read about the war in Ukraine, and become familiar with “ideas about democracy and freedom”. That awakening coincided with China’s own economic downturn . His own income, working in home renovations, fell by as much as 50% in some months.
He had long been interested in the military, but was too old to enlist in China. The decision to come to Ukraine “didn’t come out of the blue”, Vanya said. “It was the result of a lot of things building up over time: my weariness of my previous life, my longing for democracy and freedom, as well as my views on Ukraine.”
Nero, one of the Chinese volunteer soldiers
Other members of the unit claim a more fervent ideology. Nero, a 37-year-old from Fujian province, spent years posting online in support of Ukraine, becoming a well-known influencer. Several of his accounts were deleted; Nero thinks this was in response to his pro-Ukraine views.
He said the blowback he got from suspected Russian spam accounts for his support for Ukraine propelled him towards volunteering.
“I thought: the world shouldn’t be like this. Why should I suffer or go through all this just for speaking the truth?”
His move, which he publicised on social media, led to more harassment. As he arrived in Ukraine, a Russian-language “wanted” poster, which included his real name, date of birth, and picture, appeared online. The poster, which appeared to be faked, accused him of “participating in an armed conflict as a mercenary” and “illegally crossing the state border of the Russian federation”. Nero suspected it was produced by a Chinese propaganda agency working on behalf of Russia, and denied making it himself, saying that revealing his identity endangered him.
Until recently a project manager earning a decent salary in China, Nero is now training to be an FPV drone pilot. “I want people to know that not all Chinese people support Russia’s aggression. Many Chinese people, like me, are kind and want to help Ukraine,” Nero said.
L to R: Vasco, Nero, Jinmu, Chinese volunteer soldiers
All of the volunteers agreed that scrutiny from the Chinese authorities would make it difficult to return home. “If I go back now, it would be hard to leave again,” said Jinmu, a welder by trade, now working as an electrical engineer, specialising in explosives and batteries.

By MARK DUELL, DEPUTY CHIEF REPORTER (DIGITAL)
Published: 06:45 EDT, 30 September 2026 | Updated: 10:59 EDT, 30 September 2026
Prince Harry and Meghan today condemned 'extraordinarily reckless' international paparazzi who were seen looking into the grounds of their children's school.
The Duke and Duchess of Sussex 's spokesman accused two photographers of an 'unacceptable intrusion into the privacy' of Archie, seven, and Lilibet, five.
The young men were wearing backpacks and using a white van when they were spotted circling the perimeter and monitoring children by private security and school staff.
In the wake of the suspected terror plot near RAF Fairford on Sunday, a representative for the couple said the photographers' actions displayed 'an extraordinary lack of judgment'.
A number of American children with families connected to the Gloucestershire airbase, which is also used by the US Air Force, are believed to attend the school.
The spokesman for the Sussexes said: 'The decision by photographers to conduct themselves in this way around a school is extraordinarily reckless.
'There is a world of difference between legitimate media activity and photographers walking the perimeter of a school, stopping to look into the grounds and monitoring children as they go about their day.
'It is concerning enough that certain European paparazzi appear unwilling to respect the privacy of children at school.
Harry and Meghan with their children Prince Archie and Princess Lilibet in December 2025
Prince Harry and Meghan Markle at a David Foster Foundation event in Canada on August 7
'But to behave in this manner in these particular circumstances, and so soon after the incident at RAF Fairford, demonstrates an extraordinary lack of judgment.
'Whatever photographs they may have been seeking, this was not only an unacceptable intrusion into the privacy of children; it was an irresponsible and ill-considered way to conduct themselves in the vicinity of a school.'
The two men were initially seen separately and subsequently observed together before returning to a white van, which police later established was a rental vehicle.
Officers also then determined that they were international photographers working for a European press agency, which has not been named.
An insider told ITV News that the two men were seen 'scouting out' the children's school and 'doing reconnaissance' on it 'for a number of hours' before driving off.
The incident has been reported to the Executive Committee for the Protection of Royalty and Public Figures (Ravec), which is responsible for making decisions about royal security.
Harry and Meghan are waiting to hear the conclusion of Ravec's risk management board's threat assessment, which will determine whether the Sussex family should be entitled to taxpayer-funded security now they live in the UK.
The incident is understood to have taken place just 48 hours after five men were arrested near Fairford when a farmer discovered three vans blocking a road in the early hours of Sunday.
The base has been used in recent months by US bombers to launch air strikes against Iran.
Police officers guard an area near the RAF Fairford air base in Gloucestershire yesterday
Archie and Lilibet's education has already been an issue for the Sussexes, with the children moved to the new undisclosed school after just two days in class at a different institution.
The decision came after heavy traffic and the lengthy journey to the first school reportedly put their security team under strain.
The youngsters are believed to have been at their new school for around two weeks.
Harry said over the weekend that Archie and Lilibet are 'happy in school' and it is 'great' to be back in Britain – after returning a month ago following six years living in the US.
Of his return, the Prince added: 'It's been great. It's been great to be back on British soil.'
The Sussexes stepped down as working royals in 2020 for personal and financial reasons but rumours remain rife as to why they unexpectedly relocated to the UK from California.
Speculation ranges from the couple wanting their children to develop a closer relationship with their grandfather King Charles, Meghan seeking a return to acting and the Sussexes wanting to increase their profile.
In the run-up to their return, Charles was said to be glad to be able to spend more time with the family but remained adamant they would not be working royals, and there was no half-in, half-out option.
Within two weeks of arriving, there was reported pushback from Harry and Meghan after a letter, authorised by the King, was circulated by the Lord Chamberlain to senior stakeholders in the Government and military reiterating the couple were 'private citizens' and setting out guidance on how they should be treated.
The duke and duchess were said to be 'surprised' by the formal letter and the couple were reported to prefer the term 'public figures' instead.

articles.title_orig: Execution of US murderer Christa Pike halted shortly before it was due to happen
articles.title_zh: Execution of US murderer Christa Pike halted shortly before it was due to happen
articles.content_orig:
The execution of Tennessee inmate Christa Pike has been halted just over an hour before it was due to happen.
Pike, 50, has been awaiting execution since she was convicted and sentenced to death in 1996 for the murder of Colleen Slemmer.
In their ruling on Wednesday, judges from the Sixth Circuit Appeals court said they needed more time to consider the arguments in Pike's case. It is unclear how long the pause will last.
This latest ruling comes after the Supreme Court denied a reprieve and the Tennessee governor declined to grant Pike's request for clemency earlier this week.
Her lawyers said that for years, the state of Tennessee argued in court that Pike had lied about being sexually abused as a child.
But at a recent hearing about her execution method, the State said it does not dispute she suffered sexual abuse and rape.
Pike's legal team asked the appeals court to send her motion back to the district court, arguing that if the federal courts based their ruling on the state's earlier claim that she was lying, then the federal review was affected.
The appeal that led to Wednesday's stay is different from that made to the Supreme Court, which refused to hear Pike's appeal.
It came from her challenge to Tennessee's lethal injection method, which Pike's lawyers said could cause suffering beyond what is needed to carry out the death sentence - something the Constitution does not allow. The lawyers argued that Tennessee's procedures had denied Pike a fair chance to prove this.
"We will continue to advocate for the lawfully imposed sentence as the courts work through this technical issue," Tennessee's Attorney General said in a statement.
"It is common in capital cases for the defence to raise last minute objections following decades of litigation in numerous courts. We are asking the Supreme Court of the United States to lift the stay."
She was 18 when she and her then-boyfriend, Tadaryl Shipp, beat, tortured and murdered Colleen Slemmer, a 19-year-old they met at a job training camp for troubled teens.
The murder created a media frenzy in Knoxville, Tennessee in 1995, when the teen was found with a pentagram - a symbol that is associated with satanic groups - carved into her chest. Pike has denied carving the pentagram herself.
She had accused Slemmer of insulting her and trying to steal her boyfriend. Two other residents at the camp later testified that Pike had bragged about the murder before and after and showed them a piece of Slemmer's skull.
A year later, Pike was sentenced to death, while Shipp - who was 17 at the time - was given a life sentence with the possibility of parole.
Pike has a documented history of childhood sexual abuse, abandonment and neglect. Her lawyers believe that if she was found guilty of the same crime today as a teenager she would not receive a death sentence.
Last year, Tennessee's Supreme Court ruled Pike had not shown circumstances that would justify commuting her sentence.
At the time of her incarceration, Pike was the youngest person on death row, according to the Tennessee Department of Corrections.

articles.title_orig: Project B picks China as first stop for new women's basketball tour
articles.title_zh: Project B picks China as first stop for new women's basketball tour
articles.content_orig:
Project B is going to China in 2027, the women's basketball league announced on Wednesday, Sept. 30.
Hangzhou, the capital of Zhejiang province, will the first stop on the Project B's inaugural circuit. The league plans to play at the Hangzhou Olympic Sports AT Center Gymnasium from Jan. 19–24. The league announced the news with help from co-founder and chief strategy officer Russell Westbrook, co-founder and chief basketball officer Alana Beard and Chinese basketball player Li Meng.
“China has always had incredible energy around basketball, and I’ve experienced that personally throughout my career,” Westbrook said via release. “Project B is connecting basketball with culture in each place we play. I have deep respect for the history and tradition here, and also the constant drive to create what comes next. This combination is powerful.”
Training camp and Project B's first draft will be in Seoul from Jan. 6-12 ahead of players arriving in Hangzhou. The league's first season will then begin the following week. Additional details about the Hangzhou stop are expected to be announced at a later date.
“From a basketball perspective, we wanted our first stop to set the standard,” Beard said. “We’re bringing the best players in the world together to compete at the highest level, and we’re also creating an environment where they can experience new cultures and build real connections with fans. Starting in Hangzhou gives us an incredible stage for both.”
Project B's women's basketball league has more than 20 WNBA players who have signed on, including Azzi Fudd and Alanna Smith of the Dallas Wings, Alyssa Thomas of the Mercury, Awa Fam of the Seattle Storm, Jewell Loyd of the Las Vegas Aces, Jonquel Jones of the New York Liberty, Kamilla Cardoso of the Chicago Sky, Kelsey Mitchell and Sophie Cunningham of the Fever and Nneka Ogwumike , who retired from the WNBA at the end of the season.
The concept for Project B is to have two separate leagues ― men and women ― with six teams, each with 11 players. Those teams will compete in a global circuit slated to kick off in Jan. 2027 and run through April 2027. Each city will host a 10-day event, crowning a city champion, and those victories will count towards a season-long championship. Project B has revealed that, outside of Hangzhou, it will also play in Tokyo, Japan and Valencia, Spain.
Athletes who play in Project B are expected to have equity in the league. Project B hasn’t disclosed any salaries yet, but a league spokesperson previously told USA TODAY Sports they are “higher than anything you’ve ever seen in women’s sports."
The global basketball league has multiple investors, including women’s basketball legends Cheryl Miller, Candace Parker and Lauren Jackson and NFL Hall of Fame quarterback Steve Young. Additionally, Project B has secured Host Broadcast Services (HBS) to be the official broadcaster for the league’s inaugural circuit . HBS has broadcast the FIFA World Cup since 2002. The games will stream live on YouTube.

articles.title_orig: Christa Pike seeks firing squad, not lethal injection: Inside US executions
articles.title_zh: Christa Pike seeks firing squad, not lethal injection: Inside US executions
articles.content_orig:
A federal appeals court has stayed the execution of Christa Gail Pike, the only woman on the state’s “death row”, US media reported on Wednesday.
Tennessee had been set to execute the first woman in more than 200 years on Wednesday, after the United States Supreme Court rejected a bid to halt it. However, the Sixth Circuit US Court of Appeals intervened at the last minute.
Christa Pike, 50, who was convicted of torturing and killing a classmate when she was 18, was due to die by lethal injection at the Riverbend Maximum Security Institution in Nashville, but according to a report by The New York Post, she has asked to be shot by an all-female firing squad instead.
Human rights experts have condemned the decision to continue with the execution at all, but say the Supreme Court can still overturn the stay of execution.
Lawyer Clive Stafford Smith, who has represented many death row inmates in the past, told Al Jazeera: “Very few women are executed, but fewer still in Tennessee – it has been 200 years. So this is a step back to about 1820.
So why does Pike hope to avoid lethal injection in preference for the firing squad, and how does the US put people to death? Here’s what you need to know:
Pike was found guilty of the murder of another young woman she viewed as a romantic rival more than 30 years ago.
In January 1995, Pike, her 17-year-old boyfriend Tadaryl Shipp and 18-year-old Shadolla Peterson lured Colleen Slemmer, 19, into a wooded area and tortured and killed her. All four were students at a Job Corps vocational centre in Knoxville.
The case attracted huge public interest, especially after it was revealed that the attackers had carved a pentagram into Slemmer’s chest, which Shipp later admitted to carving. Pike kept a piece of Slemmer’s skull.
Pike and Shipp confessed and were convicted of first-degree murder in 1996. Pike was sentenced to death; Shipp received life with the possibility of parole.
“Christa is a 50-year-old remorseful woman who understands her actions,” her lawyers wrote.
Slemmer’s mother, May Martinez, has spoken in support of the execution.
That she should not be executed at all.
On Wednesday, just hours before Pike’s execution was due to be carried out, a federal appeals court issued an order stating: “The United States District Court for the Eastern District of Tennessee determined that it did not have jurisdiction over Christa Pike’s Federal Rule of Civil Procedure 60(b)(6) motion to reopen the judgment denying habeas relief. Therefore, it is ORDERED that execution of the sentence of death upon the movant is STAYED until further order of this court.”
However, the Supreme Court can still overturn this order, Stafford Smith told Al Jazeera. “The Supreme Court has been overturning stays recently,” he added.
Pike’s legal team previously petitioned the governor to commute her sentence to life without parole. It pointed to evidence that her mother drank heavily during pregnancy, impairing Pike’s brain development and her impulse control.
“The 18-year-old girl suffering from severe mental illness and near-debilitating trauma no longer exists,” her lawyers wrote.
She would be the only person to be executed in modern-era Tennessee for a crime committed as a teenager.
Her lawyer, Stephen Ferrell, said scientists now understand far more about adolescent brain development and that her sentence was an outlier.
Stafford Smith said: “Christa was just a teenager, and had undergone horrendous abuse as a child. Now she is 50, a totally different person. It is so pointless – will this really make the world a more civilised place?”
Governor Bill Lee has denied clemency, however. A group of United Nations human rights experts has called for her sentence to be commuted.
The US almost never executes women.
Women account for 18 of the 1,683 people executed since the Supreme Court allowed capital punishment to resume in 1976 – just more than 1 percent.
Tennessee has executed just 17 people in that time before Wednesday, with Pike the only woman on its death row.
If the execution goes ahead, it will be the state’s first execution of a woman since 1820, according to the Death Penalty Information Center.
Her legal team and trauma experts say it could force her to relive abuse she suffered in childhood.
Her clemency petition documents childhood violence, neglect and sexual abuse, including rapes when she was aged 11 and 17. It also cites her diagnoses of bipolar disorder and post-traumatic stress disorder.
Sexual violence and trauma experts argue that the procedures around lethal injection would likely trigger severe flashbacks of that abuse.
Her legal team also argues that she has small veins and a blood condition that could make it difficult to place an IV line, a claim the state disputes.
In May, Tennessee prison officials abandoned the execution of another prisoner, Tony Carruthers, after failing to find a suitable vein.
According to The New York Post, Pike’s lawyers said she also fears a painful death by lethal injection.
The paper reported that she wants to be shot by an all-female firing squad, with members of Slemmer’s family among the witnesses.
Tennessee is not among the five states that authorise the firing squad.
In court in August, her lawyers proposed hanging instead, noting it was the method Tennessee last used to execute a woman.
The state opposed that, saying Tennessee has neither the equipment nor the legal authority to carry it out. The judge sided with the state but allowed for the possibility of an all-female execution team.
Tennessee also allows prisoners whose crimes predate January 1999 to choose the electric chair; Pike’s crime took place in 1995.
There are 27 states with the death penalty, although four have placed its use on hold.
Lethal injection is authorised in every state with the death penalty; electrocution in nine states; gas in nine; and the firing squad in five. In Idaho, the firing squad became the primary method in July 2026.
Tennessee authorises lethal injection and electrocution. If both are found unconstitutional, its law allows any constitutional method.
Since 2008, the Supreme Court has required prisoners challenging an execution method to identify a feasible alternative that significantly reduces the risk of severe pain.
In June, a federal judge permanently barred Alabama from executing Jeffery Lee with nitrogen gas, ruling that it violated the Eighth Amendment’s ban on cruel and unusual punishment.
She found his proposed alternative, the firing squad, feasible.
The US has used five: lethal injection, electrocution, gas, the firing squad and hanging.
Lethal injection accounts for 1,491 executions since 1976, while electrocution has been used 163 times. Gas has been used 19 times, with Alabama and Louisiana the only states to have used it.
In nitrogen executions, a mask is placed over the prisoner’s face, and the air they breathe is replaced with pure nitrogen.
The firing squad, the method Pike reportedly wants, has been used just six times since 1976.
Hanging, once a primary method, is not currently authorised in any state.
Because none of them reliably work as intended, many experts say.
The Eighth Amendment to the US Constitution bars “cruel and unusual punishments”. But the Supreme Court has made challenges to the death penalty harder to win. It has ruled that proving a method risks severe pain is not enough; prisoners must also identify a feasible alternative that significantly reduces that risk.
Lethal injection depends on finding a usable vein. If the drugs go into a muscle instead, or the needle clogs, the prisoner can suffer extreme pain.
In 2017, legal challenges in Arkansas cited botched lethal injections in Oklahoma and Arizona.
Meanwhile, the electric chair does not always kill with the first jolt. If the prisoner’s heart is still beating, another jolt must be applied.

articles.content_orig:
Senate Democrats on Wednesday defeated a pair of bills that aimed to address data center -related affordability concerns and limit Congress members' ability to profit on the stock market while in office, arguing both were watered-down proposals.
The data center bill, dubbed the Ratepayer Protection Act failed on a vote of 57-43. A second bill, known as the Stop Insider Trading Act, which also includes a controversial voter-identification provision, was defeated on a party-line, 53-47 vote. Both bills needed 60 votes to overcome the Senate filibuster.
Republicans will likely use the votes as fodder on the campaign trail this fall, as the GOP seeks to hold  narrow majorities in both chambers despite President Donald Trump 's falling approval ratings and persistent concerns about affordability. The Senate is due to recess as soon as Wednesday, as lawmakers seeking reelection will return to their home states to campaign ahead of the 2026 midterm election .
"EVERY Senate Democrat just joined 94% of House Democrats in voting AGAINST banning congressional stock trading.," House Majority Leader Steve Scalise, R-La., posted to X immediately following the vote. The bill, he said, provides "the accountability the American people demand. But every Democrat blocked it from becoming law."
The Ratepayer Protection Act , which passed the House on a 417-3 vote earlier this month, would establish a regulatory framework that states could consider adopting to require large artificial intelligence data centers to cover their own energy costs, rather than passing them down to customers.
But Democrats have railed against the measure. Senate Minority Leader Chuck Schumer , D-N.Y., called the proposal a "toothless messaging bill" in a speech in the Senate on Tuesday.
"The bill is a fraud. I can sum up the shortcomings of Republicans' data center bill with one word: optional," Schumer said.
Sen. Elizabeth Warren , D-Mass., who has called for a national moratorium on data centers until developers can demonstrate they will cover the full cost of their construction and operation, called the legislation a "silly piece of nonsense."
"Give us something of substance and we'll vote on it," Warren said ahead of the vote.
Sen. Martin Heinrich of New Mexico, the top Democrat on the Senate Committee on Energy and Natural Resources, cited similar concerns when he blocked the bill earlier this month after Sen. Jon Husted , R-Ohio, requested unanimous consent for quick passage.
Husted is in a " toss up " race for re-election against former Democratic Sen. Sherrod Brown . Brown has accused his opponent of helping to bring data centers to the state when he was lieutenant governor.
Husted and other Republicans could use a messaging win on the data center front, which has evolved in recent months into a potent campaign issue as opponents seek stricter guardrails for developers.
Meanwhile, the congressional stock trading bill, passed the House in July on a 232-198 vote, and would prohibit sitting members of Congress from buying individual stocks. But it would not force members to divest their existing portfolios, a sticking point for some Democrats who have advocated a more stringent trading ban.
Republicans also tacked on a controversial voter identification provision to the measure, which Democrats largely oppose.
Schumer similarly criticized the stock trading proposal on Tuesday, calling it a "theatrical farce" and the voter ID provision a "poison pill."
And Sen. Tim Kaine , D-Va., said the Republican proposal was a half measure.
"It's obviously a sign that they don't take seriously the issue of insider trading. If you wanted to get a stock ban done, you would put a stock ban on the floor," Kaine said on Wednesday.
Husted, in a post to X on Tuesday, called both proposals "commonsense, bipartisan bills."
"Lowering energy costs, requiring photo ID to vote, and banning stock trading for members of Congress could be bipartisan wins," Husted wrote. "Senate Democrats are the only ones standing in the way of delivering what the American people have asked us to do."

articles.title_orig: Ethiopia fighting escalates in Tigray killing 52 civilians in Alamata, medic tells the BBC
articles.title_zh: Ethiopia fighting escalates in Tigray killing 52 civilians in Alamata, medic tells the BBC
articles.content_orig:
At least 52 civilians have been killed during three days of heavy fighting around Alamata in Ethiopia's northern Tigray region, hospital sources have told the BBC.
It appears government troops have taken control of the town from regional fighters and intend to push north towards Mekelle, the region's main city. Social media clips show army tanks on Alamata's streets.
Clashes broke out last week after months of tension between the government and the party that controls Tigray, with both accusing each other of violating a 2022 deal that ended a two-year civil war.
Fighting has also affected neighbouring regions with 33 tourists stranded for the last week in Lalibela, a Unesco world heritage site.
"We have heard fighting, gunfire and artillery cannons firing throughout the week," a British tourist, who asked not to be named, told the BBC's Newsday programme about clashes near Lalibela in the Amhara region.
He said there was a large military presence in Lalibela, famous for being home to 13th Century churches hewn from rock and a holy site for millions of Orthodox Christians.
Most visitors to the tourist hub had been unable to leave since the airport closed to commercial flights last Wednesday, though he said 14 Israeli tourists had been evacuated by military helicopter on Monday.
The fighting around Lalibela has involved the army and an Amhara militia that has allied with Tigrayan fighters.
Earlier in September, they joined forces with other Ethiopian armed movements to form a seven-member alliance with the stated intention of removing the government in the capital, Addis Ababa.
There is also a fear that neighbouring Eritrea could be drawn into the conflict - as the government accuses Asmara of supporting the armed groups, something it  denies.
The BBC is unable to report from Tigray and surrounding areas and it is difficult to find out what is happening because communications to the region have been cut.
The two sides disagree over who started the latest fighting.
The Tigray People's Liberation Front (TPLF), the party that runs Tigray, says it was responding to a federal offensive, including drone strikes, while the government says Tigrayan forces attacked first after seizing control of airports in the region.
TPLF fighters are also fighting in the Afar region, in a strategic area which connects landlocked Ethiopia to Djibouti and its ports.
Over the last few days, medical charity Médecins Sans Frontières (MSF) said more than 700 wounded people had been admitted to hospitals it supports in Tigray.
The doctor at Alamata General Hospital, who requested anonymity, told the BBC the fighting in and around the town had taken place between Saturday and Monday, and involved heavy explosives and artillery, some of which landed in residential homes.
Those killed in the crossfire included children as young as three days old, mothers and cattle herders.
Twelve people had died in a single strike on the town's marketplace, the medic said.
Since the fighting erupted, banking services in Tigray have been suspended by the government. Access to the internet has also been cut - though it is not clear who ordered the closure.
A separate source in Alamata told the BBC there was a worsening humanitarian crisis in the area, as the town swelled with people fleeing fighting.
"All the residents of the surrounding areas entered the town of Alamata by walking on foot for as long as an hour, hoping the town would be safe.
"Unfortunately, everything is blocked - no banking service, no money transfer, no power, no internet, no phone. Hence people are in crisis, simply suffering, everyone is desperate and frustrated."
The British tourist in Lalibela said online banking was working in Lalibela but there was a shortage of physical cash.
He said the situation around the town had calmed down in the last two days and there were indications the airport, which was still being used by the military, might reopen on Thursday.
"The local people, they are still scared of what might happen. The military presence here in the town has remained and a larger military force has been seen leaving the town heading north," he said.
When the airport was first closed, 53 tourists had been in the town, he explained.
But some had since been evacuated, including the 14 Israelis airlifted out on Monday while another five had left the day before via an NGO convoy, despite advice not to travel by road.
Of the remaining tourists in Lalibela, the largest group were Americans, with Israelis, Britons, South Korean, South Africans, an Ethiopian-New Zealander and a Mexican also stranded, he said.
Meanwhile, for those cut off in Tigray because of the telecoms shutdown, the Tigray Broadcasting Service (TBS), based in Addis Ababa, has started an initiative to help reconnect families.
The broadcaster has said it will collect video messages via its Telegram channel from people outside the region and air them via satellite TV.
While limited to greetings and updates, this will provide a rare lifeline for families separated by the blackout.
The clampdown on Tigray's banking services is also affecting Tigrayans who are not physically in the region.
Customers have told the BBC that bank accounts opened in Tigray have been frozen or restricted.
"I boarded public transport from Addis Ababa to Adama and tried to pay using a mobile transfer, but it didn't work," said a former Mekelle resident who moved to the capital two months ago because of growing tensions in Tigray.
"It has created havoc for many people like me who escaped the situation in Tigray," he told the BBC's Tigrinya service.
"Many Tigrayans are now in trouble."

articles.title_zh: Apple stock pops on report it will unveil all-new smart home hub at Oct. 13 event
articles.content_orig:
Oops, something went wrong
Apple ( AAPL ) stock rose in early trading on Wednesday following a report that the company is preparing to host an event next month outlining its entry into the smart home space.
According to Bloomberg's Mark Gurman , Apple will unveil an all-new smart home hub designed to control devices throughout the home, serve as a digital calendar and reminder list, play music, make video calls, and more.
Shares of Apple rose nearly 3%.
The hub, which can be mounted on a wall or placed on a counter with an accompanying stand, is designed to recognize users and provide them with personalized content via voice or facial recognition. It will also take advantage of Apple's new Siri AI platform, which it launched in beta earlier this month.
Apple is also working on a secondary version of the smart home hub featuring a robotic arm that lets the screen rotate 360 degrees.
The home hub would stand as the first new product category for Apple under CEO John Ternus , though the project has been in the works for some time. It could also serve as a lucrative new revenue stream for the company if it catches on.
Current do-it-yourself hub-style solutions require users to mount iPads to their walls to control smart home products or access them via their iPhones.
In addition to the hub, Apple is also rolling out new versions of its Apple TV set-top box and HomePod mini smart speaker. Both devices will look roughly the same as their existing versions, though they'll get more powerful processors to run Siri AI.
According to Gurman , Apple is looking to speed up its product development by making the company leaner via layoffs and other reductions.
Apple is entering a market traditionally dominated by Amazon ( AMZN ) and Google ( GOOG , GOOGL ), which had early success in the smart home space thanks to their Alexa and Google Assistant platforms, respectively.
The company's home offerings fall under its Wearables, Home, and Accessories segment, which brought in $35.68 billion in 2025, making it Apple's third-largest segment behind the iPhone and Services.
The iPhone, however, is still by far the company's most important product, bringing in $209.58 billion of Apple's $416.16 billion in total revenue last year.

articles.title_orig: Russia launches largest attack on Ukraine energy infrastructure since spring
articles.title_zh: Russia launches largest attack on Ukraine energy infrastructure since spring
articles.content_orig:
Russia has launched the largest attack on Ukraine's energy infrastructure since the spring, primarily targeting Kyiv and the surrounding region, Ukraine's Prime Minister has said.
At least five people were killed in overnight attacks across the country, including a child in the Kyiv region, Serhiy Koretskyi said.
The strikes also impacted people's power supplies, with Ukraine's biggest private energy firm DTEK saying power to 8,000 homes had been restored following "a difficult night" for the capital.
The Russian defence ministry said one of its targets was the Trypilska power station, the largest supplier of electricity to Kyiv. The operator confirmed damage to the plant.
Koretskyi wrote on Telegram: "Since the summer, there has effectively not been a single day without enemy attacks on our energy infrastructure.
"However, a mass and combined attack of this scale has occurred for the first time since the end of the last heating season."
Ukraine has been expecting another protracted Russian assault on the country's energy grid. It has happened every winter so far since Russia's full-scale invasion began in 2022.
In total, 11 regions of the country were attacked overnight, with residential buildings, social infrastructure, civilian enterprises and railways also targeted, Koretskyi said.
Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky said there had been strikes on critical infrastructure in the Zhytomyr, Mykolaiv, Kirovohrad and Rivne regions.
On Wednesday, some households in the Kyiv, Dnipropetrovsk, Donetsk, Sumy and Kharkiv regions remained without power, Ukraine's energy ministry said.
State-owned grid operator Ukrenergo advised residents not to use powerful electrical appliances between the hours of 10:00 and 16:00 local time as electricity supplies were lower than usual.
Acrid smoke obscured views over Kyiv on Wednesday
In Kyiv, people woke to find the city blanketed by thick, acrid smoke after a night punctuated by the sound of explosions. An air raid alert was still on and the distant sound of air defence gunfire echoed through the murky atmosphere.
Residents in several districts were advised to close their windows until the smoke cleared.
Among those killed in the overnight strikes was a child whose body was found under the rubble of a house, Kyiv regional head Timur Tkachenko said.
Kyiv Mayor Vitaly Klischko said three people were killed in total in the capital, including a Ukrainian utility company worker who was killed at a warehouse building.
Another person was killed in the southern Mykolaiv region, acting regional head Heorhiy Reshetilov said.
Two more people were killed in the north-eastern Sumy region on Tuesday, regional head Oleh Hryhorov said. A school was also hit there in a separate strike, he added.
Russia's defence ministry said it had launched massive overnight strikes on Ukrainian facilities.
It said targets included the Trypilska thermal power plant, located some 40km from Kyiv, and claimed the plant supplied electricity to Ukrainian defence facilities.
The operator of the plant, Centrenergo, said it was assessing the scale of the damage.
Russia's military added that it had intercepted more than 380 Ukrainian drones overnight over a number of regions, including Moscow.
Meanwhile, Ukraine's military said it had struck a number of Russian military targets, including a drone warehouse in the occupied Donetsk region in eastern Ukraine.
Russia currently controls about 20% of Ukrainian territory, including a large area of Donetsk.
On the battlefield, Ukraine's Third Army Corps said it had recaptured several settlements near the city of Lyman in Donetsk this week, as part of a counter-offensive called Operation Vivaldi. Zelensky visited troops in the area on Wednesday.
But elsewhere, the front line remains largely stagnant, with both sides failing to make significant gains.
